title: The checkpoint sweep stops at scripts/, and a dead skip arm survives in the test harness
description:
Integration gap surfaced by both tla-5zgr.1 and tla-5zgr.2 on 2026-10-08. Neither could close it alone, because the invariant spans both footprints and the two ran as a parallel wave.

THE INVARIANT AS tla-5zgr.2 RECORDED IT. No file under scripts/ OR harness/ parses a line matching ^[[:space:]]*checkpoint:, and an ORDER file containing one is a parse error rather than a skipped line.

WHAT LANDED. tla-5zgr.2 built the structural sweep at harness/test-number-problems.sh:1242 and scoped it to scripts/ only, naming tla-5zgr.1 as owner of the harness/ half. tla-5zgr.1 removed the parse from harness/sequence.sh. Verified after both merged: grep -rnE 'checkpoint:' harness/sequence.sh returns nothing.

TWO THINGS LEFT.

1. A DEAD SKIP ARM. harness/test-sequence.sh:636-645, names_in_order(), carries 'checkpoint:*) continue ;;' with the comment 'checkpoints dropped'. Under D6 an ORDER never holds a checkpoint, so the arm is unreachable, and it is exactly the shape the sweep bans. It has two callers, :816 and :1011. Remove the arm, keep the function. The sibling refusal arm at :582 is CORRECT and stays: it returns 1 with 'which D6 removed', which is a refusal and not a skip.

2. THE SWEEP SCOPE. Widen the SKIP ban to 'scripts/ harness/', with its own non-vacuity control.

DO NOT widen the LITERAL ban to harness/. The refusal tests must write 'checkpoint: ch13' and 'checkpoint: refinement' as fixture data to prove the refusal happens, and there are roughly 20 such lines across test-number-problems.sh, test-deliver-problems.sh and test-sequence.sh. Those are data, not a parse. Measured: grep -rnE 'checkpoint:' harness/ minus comment lines returns 44 lines, of which exactly one, test-sequence.sh:641, carries a continue. A blanket widen reddens the suite on legitimate fixtures.

Files: harness/test-sequence.sh, harness/test-number-problems.sh

RED: INVARIANT: no file under scripts/ or harness/ carries a line that both matches checkpoint: and skips it with continue. The sweep proves it over both directories and fails if either grep read zero files. The refusal arm at harness/test-sequence.sh:582 and the roughly 20 fixture literals under harness/ stay, so a correct fix leaves every existing assertion green.
close_reason:
Fixed in 5fc4b0d, merged. The invariant now holds across both trees, which neither tla-5zgr.1 nor .2 could close alone.

RED watched: the widened sweep caught harness/test-sequence.sh:641 'checkpoint:*) continue ;;' at 101 passed 1 failed. GREEN after removing the arm: 102 assertions.

SCOPES. Skip ban now greps scripts/ and harness/. Literal ban stays at scripts/, deliberately, because the refusal tests must write the retired spellings as fixture data.

TWO CONTROLS ADDED, and the second is the better one. The harness/ half must read at least 2 lines, and the WIDENED SCAN MUST EQUAL THE TWO HALVES SUMMED. That second control catches a typo in the wide pattern which the per-half controls would miss, which is the vacuity shape this project keeps finding.

UNTOUCHED AND VERIFIED. The refusal arm at test-sequence.sh:580-586 is absent from the diff. test-sequence.sh stayed at 51 assertions.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO THE BEAD AND TO CENTRAL'S BRIEF.

1. The bead said roughly 20 retired literals under harness/. It measures 13. The direction of the argument holds either way: widening the literal ban would redden 13 legitimate fixtures rather than 20.
2. The two-script agreement fixture is in harness/test-deliver-problems.sh at :759, asserting 02_probe-bonded:5, NOT in test-number-problems.sh as central's brief implied. Outside the footprint and not in the commit, so it was never at risk, but the brief named the wrong file.

The 44-lines-one-continue measurement reproduced exactly at HEAD: 18 in test-number-problems.sh, 15 in test-sequence.sh, 11 in test-deliver-problems.sh, one continue. It reads 47 now and the delta is this bead's own two new greps and their message lines.

title: Drop the checkpoint markers from the order machinery
description:
D6, the order-machinery half. Design: drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_20ad6fe9661059e6d830b053.

Under D6 the two positional markers stop existing, so every file that parses one drops the parse.

  scripts/number-problems.sh:119-126   skips blank lines, # comments, and exactly
                                       "checkpoint: ch13" and "checkpoint: refinement"
  scripts/deliver-problems.sh          same skip list
  harness/test-number-problems.sh      fixtures and assertions covering the skip
  harness/test-deliver-problems.sh     same

THE ONE THING THAT MUST SURVIVE. A marker took a POSITION without consuming a NUMBER, which is why ORDER's line number is not the position. Blank lines and # comments still do that, so the line-number-is-not-the-position property stays true and its tests stay. The tla-6mrz worker gated that agreement by handing one ORDER to both scripts and requiring identical names out of each, with a fixture putting probe-bonded on raw line 5 at position 2. Keep that fixture and that gate. Only the two checkpoint rows come out.

Also keep scripts/number-problems.sh:174-176, which widens the field past two digits. Unrelated to this change.

grep -c 'checkpoint:' over the live ~/tla-practice/problems/ORDER returns 0 over a 7-line file, so nothing delivered regresses.

RED: INVARIANT: no file under scripts/ or harness/ parses a line matching ^[[:space:]]*checkpoint:, and an ORDER file containing one is a parse error rather than a skipped line. The existing property that a blank line and a # comment occupy no position still holds, proven by the two-script agreement fixture.

Files: scripts/number-problems.sh, scripts/deliver-problems.sh, harness/test-number-problems.sh, harness/test-deliver-problems.sh
close_reason:
Both ORDER parsers now refuse a checkpoint: line instead of skipping it. Landed 158b2cd, merged to main. number-problems.sh exits 2 (the input-is-unusable class, alongside a missing root and a missing ORDER), deliver-problems.sh exits 1, which is the only failure code its contract has; the asymmetry was kept rather than inventing a code and is commented in both files. The pattern is the whole checkpoint: prefix, not the two retired literals, because a tail nobody retired is still a line neither script can give a position to.

RED watched failing first: 12 failures in the number suite, 11 in the deliver suite. GREEN at 100 and 101 assertions, up from 84 and 88, +29 total. Full gate green, 20 suites, 187.8s.

What survived, verified: number-problems.sh width-widening untouched, and the two-script agreement gate unchanged and passing with probe-bonded still on raw line 5 at position 2. A comment and a blank now hold the lines the markers sat on, so every position-to-raw-line pair is byte-identical. The live ORDER carries no checkpoint line, and better evidence than the grep is that --check against the live tree exits 0 after the change with 01_bonded-store through 07_estate-notice in step.

THE FINDING WORTH KEEPING. The bead was stronger than its own design drawer and that was right. D6's L3 spec says only 'no file parses one', which a bare arm-removal satisfies. The bead said 'is a parse error', and the RED run showed why: a bare removal fails SILENTLY in deliver-problems.sh, where the marker becomes an entry, takes a position, shifts everything below it down one, and the run exits 0 having delivered out of an unparseable line. A spec that says what must not be parsed does not say what must happen instead.

Process note: the structural sweep stayed red after the fix because it matched its own refusal arm. 'Parses one' and 'is a parse error' are opposites, so banning the word bans the refusal too. The corrected sweep drops comment lines, then bans the two accept-shapes, and both patterns were proven against the real pre-change code.

The harness/ half of the invariant is filed as tla-ec2o, which neither this bead nor .1 could close alone.

title: sequence.sh: drop clause (c), and split the report into ramp rungs and reserve candidates
description:
D6 and D7 both land in harness/sequence.sh, so they are one bead. Design: drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_20ad6fe9661059e6d830b053.

TWO CHANGES, ONE FILE.

D6's ORDER half. Clause (c) comes out of the sequence invariant. The script stops reading a record's gate line, so GATE_RE and its parse go, and the two checkpoint lines stop being placed. Today --search places them by construction (the header comment at harness/sequence.sh:52-58 says so) and only --check enforces them, so removing the placement and the clause is symmetrical work.

D7's report split. A failed search currently prints "no valid order over N problems" and lists every unplaced record as a violation. title: [epic] Cycle 5: the reading gate becomes a label, and the course gets published
description:
Handoff from cycle 5 of the difficulty-progression design cycle, 2026-10-03.

Design source of truth: drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_20ad6fe9661059e6d830b053 (cycle 5's working surface, Tier-0 green, four locked decisions D6 to D9). The cycle's own STATE HEADER lives on drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_4cd7acae35ef634cf4ebbabb.

WHY THIS CYCLE REOPENED A GREEN ONE. Cycle 4 locked D1 to D5 on 2026-09-04 and went green. On 2026-10-02 the audience changed from Frank to anyone who has finished learntla, which removed the premise of D4 clause (c), the reading gate. Reopening also turned up F1, which refutes a claim central had been acting on for a day.

F1, AND IT IS THE REASON TO READ THE DRAWER BEFORE ANY CHILD HERE. The ramp is NOT wedged. harness/sequence.sh --search reasons over 13 vector records and six of those are exactly the problems D5 withdrew on 2026-09-04. Point VECTOR_ROOT at a tree holding the floor plus the seven authored-to-rung problems and it returns the live ORDER and exits 0. The true state is seven rungs built, position 8 unauthored.

THE FOUR DECISIONS.

  D6  the reading gate is a label, not an ordering rule        -> .1 (ORDER half), .2, .3 (field half)
  D7  --search keeps the withdrawn set and labels it           -> .1
  D8  references get their own top-level section               -> .4

title: The refinement chapter and the worked example are written, verified, and unpublished
description:

MEASURED 2026-10-03.

  chapter/refinement.md       816 lines, 5520 words
  chapter/worked-example.md   410 lines, 2259 words
  chapter/snippets/            45 files

Both authored under tla-kl5.1 and verified under tla-kl5.2, every snippet executed and every quotation traced. Both beads closed.

scripts/build-docs.sh publishes exactly two source trees, exercises/ and module-docs/. chapter/ is in neither, so the whole directory is dark. Probed live:

  https://fkberthold.github.io/tla-puzzles/refinement/           404

The reading gate. title: Problems have no delivery script, so what ships is written down nowhere
description:
Exercises have scripts/deliver-exercises.sh, which states at :20-26 exactly what it hands over and what it withholds, and harness/test-deliver-exercises.sh gates it. Problems have nothing. ls scripts/ | grep -i deliver returns one file and it is the exercises one.

So the delivered contents of a problem exist only as whatever was copied by hand on the day it shipped. The authoritative manifest turns out to be everything under authoring/<name>/statement/, but nothing in the repo says so and the shape is not uniform:

  01_bonded-store    PROBLEM.md, traces/ x5, BondedStore.tla
  02_laytime         PROBLEM.md, traces/ x3
  03_river-call      PROBLEM.md, traces/ x3, RiverCall.cfg
  04_assay-office    PROBLEM.md, traces/ x6, AssayOffice.tla
  05_floor-malting   PROBLEM.md, traces/ x7
  06_herbarium-sheet PROBLEM.md, traces/ x7
  07_estate-notice   PROBLEM.md, traces/ x8

Three of the seven ship a starter artifact and four do not, because representation 1 on the load vector means the problem HANDS the learner a spec and representation 2 means the learner writes it. 01 and 04 are the representation-1 problems and ship a .tla. 03 ships only a .cfg. There is no starters/ directory anywhere under authoring/, so a reader looking for the convention finds none.

HOW THIS BIT, 2026-10-02. Frank asked for the attempts backed up and the problems reset to pristine. I cleaned the delivered tree by removing everything that was not PROBLEM.md, ATTEMPT-LOG.md or traces/, on the reasoning that the rest was his work. That deleted three SHIPPED files: 01s BondedStore.tla, 03s RiverCall.cfg and 04s AssayOffice.tla. Frank caught it by reading 01s PROBLEM.md, which says at :15 "BondedStore.tla: the model" and at :22 to write properties INTO it.

Everything was recoverable, from the verified backup and from the repo, and the tree now diffs clean against every statement/ directory. But I had also reported 03 as "a config for a module you never wrote" and 04 as "a module you never ran", and both of those were the shipped artifact rather than a partial attempt. So the wrong manifest produced a wrong reading of his progress, which is the more expensive failure.

ALSO: the nine ATTEMPT-LOG.md files were not in the repo at all until 22a181b earlier the same day. That is the same gap one layer along.

THE WORK. Write scripts/deliver-problems.sh with the same posture as the exercises one: state what it delivers and what it withholds, in the file, and never overwrite an existing file. Then a gate that compares a fresh delivery against authoring/<name>/statement/ so the manifest cannot drift from the script.

Two things it has to get right that the exercises script does not face. A problem is delivered under its NUMBERED directory name (01_bonded-store), which scripts/number-problems.sh owns, so the script needs the ORDER position rather than the bare name. And an unnumbered problem is off the ramp by convention, so the script has to handle both.

RED: INVARIANT: a freshly delivered problem directory contains exactly the files under that problem authoring/<name>/statement/, and delivering over an existing directory changes no file already there.

Files: scripts/deliver-problems.sh, harness/test-deliver-problems.sh
close_reason:
GREEN and merged. RED a818390, GREEN 0dd907b, SUITES row 7fce2bd, all on main, pushed 71a6f97..7fce2bd. Full gate green, 20 suites, 286.9s. The suite reads OK: 88 assertions passed.

scripts/deliver-problems.sh copies everything under <location>/<name>/statement/ recursively, so the manifest IS the tree and cannot drift from a list. It resolves a name across authoring/, curated/ and sources/problems/, and fails loudly on zero matches, on two or more, and on a directory with no statement/ (which is live: authoring/museum/ holds only DESCRIPTION.md). Never overwrites, per file, matching deliver-exercises.sh:100-108.

End to end: delivering all seven into a temp root and running diff -r against the live ~/tla-practice/problems gives rc=0 and no output. Byte for byte, numbering and all three starter artifacts.

THE MUTATION IS WHY THIS IS TRUSTWORTHY. The worker planted the exact guess I made by hand earlier today, filtering to PROBLEM.md plus ATTEMPT-LOG.md plus traces/*, and re-ran. 8 rows fired, including the original bug reproduced as 'Only in authoring/bonded-store/statement: BondedStore.tla'. And the instructive half: its uniform-shape fixture stayed GREEN under that mutation, because against a uniform tree a list and a tree are indistinguishable. The discriminating rows are a fixture copying the real bonded-store tree plus a SURPRISE.tla, a nested extra/nested/DEEP.md and a planted author-notes file, plus one row that delivers the real bonded-store into a temp dest. Three further rows assert the mutation itself, so a fixture that lost its discriminating files cannot quietly re-admit a list.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO MY BRIEF, both measured rather than argued.

1. ORDER positions are not line numbers. scripts/number-problems.sh:119-126 skips blank lines, # comments, and the markers 'checkpoint: ch13' and 'checkpoint: refinement', none of which consume a position, and :174-176 widens past two digits. The worker matched the script rather than the brief and GATED the agreement: the suite hands one ORDER to both scripts and requires identical directory names out of each, over comments, blanks, leading whitespace and both markers. Its fixture ORDER puts probe-bonded on raw line 5 at position 2, and five rows assert that gap. Recorded on tla-jaob.2, because it sharpens the N4 reading-gate question: the checkpoint mechanism is implemented in six files and the live ORDER carries zero of them.

2. There are TWO PROBLEM-with-author-notes.md files, not one. curated/majority-vote/statement/ and sources/problems/fencing/statement/. My brief named only the curated one, so an exclusion list written from it would have shipped fencing's author notes to a learner. The worker took the *-with-author-notes.md convention instead, which also matches existing authoring/custody/author-notes/ and authoring/seedlib/author-notes/ usage, and reports every withheld file as 'withheld (author notes): <path>' so a withholding is never silent.

NO TEST TOUCHED THE REAL PRACTICE TREE. Every run passes an explicit dest-root under a fresh mktemp -d and redirects HOME. The default-root section runs only --check. Source resolution happens before any mkdir, so all six fatal paths create nothing. Confirmed after the fact with find ~/tla-practice -newermt '-120 minutes' returning nothing.

Two things the worker added unasked and justified: a --check mode, borrowing the flag name from number-problems.sh, which is what makes the default-root probe safe without running anything mutating; and a refusal when the destination already holds the problem under a DIFFERENT number, which would otherwise create two directories for one ORDER entry and make number-problems.sh report 'ambiguous' forever.

FILED FROM IT: tla-ly1p (P2), a dispatched worker has nowhere safe to put a scratch file, since the environment prompt names the session scratchpad and edit-write-pwd-guard refuses writes there from a worktree.

title: The full gate spends 76 percent of its wall clock enforcing retired rules
description:
Measured 2026-10-01 against two consecutive full gate runs at 298.5s and 296.5s.

PRACTICE-PLAN.md:159-168 retires nine things. Six of them have a suite in the scripts/test SUITES table that runs on every full gate.

| suite | scripts/test row | measured | retired item, verbatim |
|---|---|---|---|
| puzzle screen | :174 harness/screen.sh --selftest | 1.0s | "The domain and puzzle screens" |
| vector records | :196 harness/test-vector.sh | 0.6s | "The load vector" |
| ramp sequence | :201 harness/test-sequence.sh | 1.6s | "the ramp rule" |
| vacuity gate | harness/test-vacuity.sh | 88.0s | "The vacuity probes" |
| seeded-bug matrix | harness/fixtures/seeded-bugs/selftest.sh | 53.8s | "The seeded-bug matrix" |
| grader | harness/grade.sh --selftest | 79.2s | "The grader and its verdict objects" |

Sum 224.2s of 296.5s. That is 75.6 percent.

Add the refinement harness at 19.6s and it is 243.8s, 82.2 percent. Refinement is not in the bullet list but PRACTICE-PLAN.md:67 names it in prose: "About 3,800 lines of grading, vacuity, refinement and seeded-bug harness stop being maintained."

One suite is ambiguous and I am leaving it out of the count. The TLC verdict channel (harness/test-verdict.sh, 17.8s) could be read against "The grader and its verdict objects", but .claude/rules/dispatched-agents.md records harness/verdict.sh as shared infrastructure that every component TLC invocation goes through, so it may outlive the grader.

WHY THIS IS NOT ALREADY COVERED BY THE PLAN. PRACTICE-PLAN.md:157 says "Retired means nobody maintains it. Nothing is deleted." And :67-68 says the harnesses "stop being maintained. Nothing is deleted. It sits in the repo and nobody feeds it."

Sitting in the repo and running on every gate are different things. A reader of that line would not expect three quarters of their gate wall clock to be it. Nobody feeds these suites and all six still vote.

THE LIVE HAZARD, which is not the wall clock. A green unmaintained gate is a trap in two directions:

1. It reads as authoritative. That already cost a design cycle. See tla-t8jz: the 09-21 prose-pipeline cycle read the load vector as the live placement authority, locked four decisions and filed five beads, and only the plan file said otherwise.
2. One of them going red blocks all work on a rule nobody believes in. 221 of the 224 seconds are the three heaviest suites in the gate, and they are the three the plan is most explicit about.

STRANDED WORK ON ONE OF THEM. Branch worktree-agent-a861e0f7ccafa0cae holds commit d6a8dc1, dated 2026-09-04, "WIP salvaged by /cleanup-orphans 2026-09-05". It carries 222 changed lines in harness/screen.sh, 201 in harness/fixtures/screen/selftest.sh, and a new 30-line threshold-README.md. It has never been merged. harness/screen.sh on main was last touched 2026-08-07 at e87de77 and is still gated at scripts/test:174 with 71 assertions. So there is a substantial unmerged improvement to a component the plan retired the next day.

Two sibling orphan branches hold review reports rather than code, and both are about work the same day retired. worktree-agent-a56372d6ec7191fab has b5zh-verify-verdict.md, 350 lines, verdicts on authoring/qsl, buyclub and consign DESCRIPTION.md. worktree-agent-a67d3c0eba4951452 has b5zh-fit-review.md, 695 lines. Those three problems went to the reserve under D5 of the difficulty-progression cycle on 2026-09-04. I read the head of the first report and it is a clean verification pass, not scratch.

THE DECISION IS FRANK-S AND IT IS THE SAME SHAPE AS tla-t8jz:
1. Un-retire some of these, in which case say which and the suites keep voting.
2. Retire the suites with the rules. Move the six rows out of the SUITES table, keep the scripts in the repo as the plan promises, and the full gate drops to about 72s.
3. Something in between, most likely keeping whatever turns out to be shared infrastructure rather than a retired rule. harness/verdict.sh is the clear case.

I lean toward 2 for everything except whatever proves to be shared. A gate nobody feeds is worse than no gate, because it looks like a guarantee. But this reverses nothing measured, so it is cheap to change back, and the scripts are not deleted either way.

BEFORE ANY OF IT: decide what happens to d6a8dc1. If the screens come back it wants merging. If they do not it wants recording and deleting, and this bead is the record.

DEPENDS ON NOTHING, but tla-t8jz is the narrow version of the same question and should be answered in the same sitting.

AUTOFAN-EXCLUDE: needs a ruling from Frank, not a dispatch.

Files: scripts/test, PRACTICE-PLAN.md
notes:
---
ONE FIELD HAS A LIVE CONSUMER, found 2026-10-01 while auditing the open P1 queue.

The load-vector record carries three non-numeric fields: situation, task shape, and reading gate (ch11 | ch13 | refinement), added as D4 of the difficulty-progression cycle.

tla-h1ki is a live consumer of the reading gate and the only one I found. It measures that six of seven delivered batch-2 references need a chapter-12 construct (EXCEPT counts 4, 5, 4, 5, 7, 4, 0) while all seven declare a chapter-11 gate. Its defect rests on the exercise set own words, exercises/ch11/EXERCISES.md and exercises/ch13/EXERCISES.md, neither of which is retired, so the defect survives the retirement. What does not survive is the field it reads the declared gate OFF.

So if option 2 is taken and the vector record goes, tla-h1ki becomes unmeasurable rather than fixed. Nothing would record which chapter a problem needs.

That argues for a narrower option than I first wrote: retire the suites that enforce retired rules, but keep the reading gate under some owner, which could be as small as one line in each problem statement rather than a six-dimension record. I did not find a live consumer for the six numeric dimensions or for situation and task shape in the same audit, though I only read the open P1 beads, so treat that as a gap in my search rather than a proof of absence.

---
FRANK RULED 2026-10-02 on the ramp half only: "Agreed, they matter."

So of the six suites enforcing retired rules, THREE are rescued and keep voting: vector records 0.6s, ramp sequence 1.6s, and the ch11 floor they rest on. Those are the three cheapest.

The expensive three are NOT rescued and still need a ruling: vacuity gate 88.0s, grader 79.2s, seeded-bug matrix 53.8s. That is 221 of the 224 seconds. The grader got DEADER under the audience change rather than less dead: 69 to 71 percent over-validation, and a stranger has nobody to appeal to.

So this bead narrows usefully. Un-retire the ramp machinery, then the only question left is whether three suites totalling 221 seconds keep running on rules nobody feeds. That is a much easier call than the one I filed.

Still open and still Frank: the unmerged 424-line improvement to harness/screen.sh on branch worktree-agent-a861e0f7ccafa0cae, dated the day before the screens were retired. The screens are not rescued by the audience change either.

UNBLOCKED 2026-10-15 by Frank's ruling on tla-jaob: he stays the only
audience, so PRACTICE-PLAN.md's premises stand and the nine retirements at
:159-168 are live rather than suspect.

That was the only thing in the way. This bead proposes deleting six suites on
the strength of retirements recorded in that document, and until tonight the
P0 said the document's premises were invalidated by an audience change.

RE-MEASURE BEFORE CUTTING ANYTHING. The 76 percent figure comes from two full
gate runs at 298.5s and 296.5s on 2026-10-01. The gate is now 36 suites at
410.5s, measured 2026-10-15 on a quiet box, so both the numerator and the
denominator have moved and the percentage is a two-week-old reading rather
than a current one. Four suites have been added since: drill style measure,
construct coverage map, and re-bases on drill study check and reading corpus
gate.

AND CHECK EACH RETIREMENT AGAINST THE SUITE, not against the table. A suite
whose row name matches a retired item may still be the only thing gating
something else that was never retired. The six rows this bead names were
matched by what they enforce, and matching by name is the staleness shape this
project has hit four times tonight alone.
THE 76 PERCENT IS STALE, AND NOT BECAUSE ANYTHING GOT CHEAPER. Re-measured 2026-10-17 against the full registry at 719.4s, 39 suites green on a quiet box (load 2.4), after the recall rung landed.

  puzzle screen        1.5s
  vector records       1.2s
  ramp sequence        1.7s
  vacuity gate        50.8s
  seeded-bug matrix   50.8s
  grader              87.7s
  ------------------------
  sum                193.7s of 719.4s  =  26.9 percent

With the refinement harness at 11.1s it is 204.8s, 28.5 percent.

The six retired-rule suites cost about what they did (193.7 tonight against 224.2 on 2026-10-01, and the box reads a touch faster across the board). The DENOMINATOR more than doubled: 296.5s to 719.4s. The recall rung is 282.7s of the new total on its own, the recall corpus gate alone 194.7s, which is now the registry's dearest row ahead of the grader.

So the headline in this bead's title is wrong by a factor of nearly three and the share is still 194 seconds of real time. Both of those are true at once and they point different ways on priority. Worth re-reading before anyone acts on the P1.

Not acted on. Numbers only.
2026-10-18, central. THE HEADLINE NUMBER IS STALE AND THE SHARE IS NOW 23.5 PERCENT, NOT 76.

The description measured 224.2 s of 296.5 s on 2026-10-01. Re-measured today off the registry's own budgets:

  bash scripts/test --list  ->  44 suites, 944.2 s of budget in total

  puzzle screen        1.5
  vector records       1.3
  ramp sequence        2.0
  vacuity gate        60.0
  seeded-bug matrix   57.8
  grader              99.0
                    ------
                     221.6 s, which is 23.5 percent of 944.2

Add the refinement harness at 12.9 and it is 234.5 s, 24.8 percent. The last full run central measured on a quiet box was 837.3 s.

The six suites did not grow. The GATE did, by roughly a factor of three, so the retired share fell without anybody touching it. The wall-clock argument in the description has mostly dissolved and should not be quoted as it stands.

WHAT SURVIVES INTACT is the hazard argument, which was always the stronger half: a green unmaintained gate reads as authoritative, and it already cost a design cycle when the 09-21 prose-pipeline cycle read the load vector as the live placement authority, locked four decisions and filed five beads. Nothing about that changes with the percentage.

So this bead is still worth doing and it is no longer a performance bead. Reprice it as a correctness one when it is picked up.

title: A delivered problem is either on the ramp with a package or declared off it
description:
Goal: close the silent hole. Today a prose problem can be delivered with no
ramp package and nothing notices, because the ramp's invariant only reaches
problems whose reference is frozen.

From D1 of `drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_0721f0abe841f73eb9def38d`.

`scripts/number-problems.sh` already walks the delivered tree and already
distinguishes numbered from unnumbered, so it is the natural home. A numbered
directory must resolve to a package. An unnumbered one must be named in an
explicit list, so that "outside the ramp" is a recorded decision rather than an
absence.

Where the list lives is open. A sibling file next to `ORDER` is the obvious
shape and matches how `ORDER` already works. Pick it or argue for better.

RED: INVARIANT: every directory in the delivered problems tree either carries a numeric prefix and resolves to a VECTOR.md with reference/FREEZE.sha256 beside it, or carries no prefix and is named in an explicit outside-the-ramp list.

Note the resolution has to cross out of the delivered tree into the repo, which
nothing in `scripts/number-problems.sh` does yet. It takes a problems-root
argument and knows nothing about `authoring/`. Decide whether it grows a second

title: The prose pipeline emits a ramp record
description:
The prose pipeline builds problems the ramp cannot see. It emits no frozen
reference and no `VECTOR.md`, so `harness/sequence.sh` refuses any `ORDER` entry
naming one, and `fencing` sits delivered and unnumbered.

Design cycle `drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_0721f0abe841f73eb9def38d`, cycle 1,
Tier-0 green. Four decisions, each with a Tier-1 invariant that becomes a child
bead's RED test.

- D1, a prose problem's ramp package lives in `authoring/<name>/`.
- D2, the frozen reference answers the statement's own "What to produce".
- D3, a spike's 1-to-5 estimate is labelled candidate-selection-only.
- D4, the vector author is a separate read-only step after the freeze.

Why nothing flagged this, which is the finding worth keeping. The ramp's own
invariant reads "every authored problem WHOSE REFERENCE IS FROZEN carries a
vector record". A problem that skips freezing skips the clause, so the gate
never fired and the guarantee was never wrong.

The pipeline gains three steps after the consistency check, mirroring batch 2's
steps 3, 4 and 9. Copy the reference out per D2 and strip its comments, freeze
the stripped form, have a separate reader write `VECTOR.md` from the frozen
statement and frozen reference, then a gated comment pass and the ramp gates.

Depends on `tla-frpu`. The six pipeline steps exist only in
`sources/run-2026-09-06/PLAN.md`, a dated run record, and `PRACTICE-PLAN.md:134`
still reads "One scale, anchored on state representation" from the day before
the direction change. A gate enforcing a step should not land before the step is
written down.

updated first.

title: number-problems.sh ignores mv failures, so a half-applied rename reports success
description:
`scripts/number-problems.sh` never checks whether a `mv` worked. Phase 3 is two
loops of bare `mv`, and the script runs under `set -uo pipefail` with no `-e`, so
a failed rename is skipped and the script still exits 0.

```
for i in "${!plan_src[@]}"; do
  mv -- "$PROBLEMS_ROOT/${plan_src[$i]}" "$PROBLEMS_ROOT/${plan_dst[$i]}$tmp_suffix"
done
```

`scripts/number-problems.sh:198-205`.

The contract this was built against says exit 1 on "a rename that could not
complete". That clause is unimplemented. Found at central's verify step for
`tla-0lwx`, after the suite went green, because no assertion covers it.

## Why it matters more here than it looks

The fail-closed design of `tla-0lwx` exists because `~/tla-practice` is not a git
repo and holds attempt work that does not come back. Phase 2 earns that by
validating everything before moving anything. Phase 3 then gives it away: a `mv`
that fails partway leaves exactly the half-applied tree the refusal was built to
prevent, and reports success while doing it.

Worse than a half-applied tree, it can leave directories parked under the
`.number-problems-tmp.$$` suffix from the first loop. Those are invisible to
`--check`, because the sweep only looks at names carrying a `^[0-9]+_` prefix.

## What to do

Check each `mv`. On a failure, report which rename failed and exit 1. Whether to
attempt a rollback of the renames already applied is a real question and I do not
think it is obvious. Rolling back is more code running at the moment things are
already going wrong. Stopping and telling the human names the exact state the tree
is in, which may be the better trade on a tree a person owns.

A test needs a `mv` that fails on purpose. Making the destination parent
unwritable with `chmod` is the usual way, and it needs a skip when the suite runs
as root, where the permission bit is ignored.

## One latent thing, worth a look while in there

`${name}` is interpolated straight into an ERE at `scripts/number-problems.sh:117`
and `:150`. Every current problem name is lowercase letters and hyphens, so nothing
misbehaves today. A name carrying a `.` or a `+` would match more than itself.

Files: scripts/number-problems.sh, harness/test-number-problems.sh
close_reason:
Merged at 296429c, worker commit fcfcab6.

Every mv is checked now. On a failure the run names the rename, says which entries are done, parked or untouched, names the temp suffix when something is actually parked, and exits 1. Nothing is rolled back, which is a decision rather than a gap: a rollback is more code running while the tree is already wrong, and this tree has no history behind it.

Entry matching is literal rather than an interpolated ERE. matches_entry replaces both regex sites.

CORRECTION to what this bead claimed. I wrote that --check could not see a stranded temp directory because the sweep only matches a numeric prefix. That is wrong, and the worker probed it before writing anything: a parked name carries the prefix too, so the numbered-stranger sweep already caught it and exited 1. The hole was the diagnosis rather than the exit code. A reader was told ORDER does not name the directory, which sends them to edit ORDER when what happened is a run died mid-rename. Implemented as a message fix, and it is the only assertion in the suite that pins message text.

Also from the worker, better than what I briefed: a plain file sitting on the destination name blocks an mv as any user, where chmod is ignored under root. Both fixtures kept, with visible SKIP rows rather than silent passes.

VERIFICATION: harness/test-number-problems.sh 84 assertions rc=0, up from 64. bash scripts/test 18 suites in 245.8s rc=0. bash scripts/lint clean over 40 files. harness/test-pipefail.sh 24 assertions rc=0.

title: fencing has no load-vector record, so the ramp cannot place it
description:
`fencing` sits in `~/tla-practice/problems/` and cannot enter `ORDER`.
`harness/sequence.sh` resolves every `ORDER` entry against a `VECTOR.md` record in
this repo, and an entry with no record is a hard exit 2 rather than a warning. See
`harness/sequence.sh:591`.

The scan finds records by looking for `reference/FREEZE.sha256` under `authoring/`
and `pilot/`, then reading the `VECTOR.md` one level up. `fencing` has neither. It
was built through the prose pipeline of 2026-09-06, which writes
`sources/problems/fencing/` and `sources/spikes/fencing/` and emits no load-vector
record at all.

So the new pipeline builds problems the ramp cannot see. `fencing` is the first, and
every prose problem after it has the same gap.

## What to build

Give `fencing` an `authoring/fencing/` package of the shape batch 2 uses.
`reference/` holds the chosen module, its `.cfg` and `FREEZE.sha256`. `VECTOR.md`
carries the six dimensions cited against that reference and the shipped statement,
plus the situation, task shape and reading gate lines. `authoring/bonded-store/` is
the model to copy.

The open question is which module is the reference. `sources/spikes/fencing/` holds
about 30 modules across broken, fenced, abstract, unbounded and restart variants.
Picking one is a judgment call, and I don't think it should be made without reading
the spike report first.

Once the record exists, `harness/sequence.sh --search` places `fencing` on merit and
it takes a number under the sibling bead.

## The wider gap

I'd fix `fencing` first and treat the pipeline question as separate. Every prose
problem needs this record, and the honest fix is for the pipeline to emit one rather
than for someone to backfill each time. That's worth its own bead once we've done
one by hand and know what it costs.

title: Problem directories carry no order, so ORDER is the only place it lives
description:
Ten directories sit in `~/tla-practice/problems/` and nothing in a name says which
to work next. That lives in `ORDER`, a separate file, and the two have already come
apart. `ORDER` lists 7 and the tree holds 10.

Frank, 2026-09-18: get the order into the directory name, `#_name`.

## The design

`ORDER` stays the one source of truth. A line's position in the file is its number,
and directory names are derived from that position. `bonded-store` at line 1 becomes
`01_bonded-store`. Two digits, because the plan runs to about 48 problems and `1_`
sorts wrong at ten.

The alternative is to write the number into the `ORDER` entries as well. I'd avoid
it. The position would then sit in the file twice, once as the line number and once
as the prefix, and those two can disagree. Keeping the entries bare also leaves
`harness/sequence.sh` alone, and that gate passes today.

A directory with no number is a problem outside the ramp. Two are there now.
`fencing` waits on a load-vector record and gets its number when that lands.
`majority-vote` is out of the ramp by Frank's call of 2026-09-18, and stays
unnumbered.

## What to build

- `scripts/number-problems.sh`, reads `ORDER` and renames to match.
- `harness/test-number-problems.sh`, the gate, registered in `scripts/test`.
- The rename, run once against the real tree.

The gate has to catch three shapes. A numbered directory that `ORDER` does not name.
A number that disagrees with its `ORDER` position. An `ORDER` entry with no
directory behind it.

`scripts/deliver-exercises.sh` is the precedent for taking a destination root and
defaulting under `$HOME`. `harness/test-deliver-exercises.sh` sandboxes `HOME` so
the real tree is never touched, and this suite needs the same.

## Two cautions

`~/tla-practice` is not a git repo, so a bad rename doesn't come back. Frank has
live attempt state in `bonded-store` and `fencing`.

`README.md` steps 2 to 4 make `attempts/<name>/` and `released/<name>/` mirror
`problems/<name>/`. Those two trees go out of step the moment this lands. Renaming
them is out of scope by Frank's call, and I think it wants a follow-up bead.

Merged at b56b8e4 (implementation) and a271c4f (RED suite), budget corrected at 28f299e. Drawer drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_ac8bd4ec4177c09a33fe243e.

The rename is applied. ~/tla-practice/problems now reads 01_bonded-store through 07_estate-notice, with fencing and majority-vote unnumbered because they sit outside the ramp. Frank gave the go on 2026-09-18 after seeing the rehearsal.

title: Build a workflow problem, the shape only issue trackers supply
description:
Workflow is the shape this engineer needs most, and general issue trackers are the only
source that carries it. Postmortems returned zero across 240 triaged and 27 read. Jepsen
has about one instance in 50 analyses. Evidence in sources/issues.md and
sources/postmortems.md.

Five instances found. The two strongest:

KAFKA-20090, a transaction that can neither commit nor time out, with a four-step sequence
given in prose.

temporal 10639, a parent aborts and a child finishes anyway, and a restart never sees it.

Both are multi-step multi-party sequences with real abort branches, which is what the
yardstick means by workflow and what his platform's hardest bugs look like: the narrator
deploy flow with three sequential per-asset approvals and an explicit reject path, and the
IAM invitation whose every transition is guarded by current status.

Temporal is the richest tracker found anywhere in the survey, and the reason is worth
knowing because it inverts the obvious heuristic. It has one body hit for the word
invariant. CockroachDB has 171 and is unusable, all storage internals. What predicts yield
is an issue template with an expected-behaviour heading plus protocol-shaped subject
matter, not the vocabulary.

Holding the cause back is a heading-level deletion in 20 of 24 cases.

Judged from prose with nothing built. Spike before committing to either.

title: Package the isolation family: give the scaffolding, build the ladder
description:
The spike settled the question the family turned on. Modelling the mechanism is dead,
since the published reference reaches a read-only anomaly at 405,673,796 distinct states
in 64 minutes. Modelling the application against a permitted-interleaving oracle finds
write skew at 21 states and half a second. Evidence in sources/spikes/isolation/REPORT.md.

What makes this a family rather than one problem is that the scaffolding can be handed
over. Each application was written once and generated for the other levels by substituting
two tokens, and diff between two levels returns two lines with the configs byte-identical.
So the learner gets one module per isolation level plus an eight-name interface, and
writes only the application.

Three things to do.

Package the given part. IsoSerial, IsoSnapshot and IsoReadCommitted plus the interface,
with a note saying what a learner may assume about each and what it deliberately does not
model.

Write two more applications. The spike has three and the ladder needs more to be proven
rather than promising. Write skew alone cannot separate the levels, since read committed
and snapshot both permit it, so the ladder runs on two axes, level and anomaly, with
constants as a separate size knob.

Decide what the learner is asked to produce. The natural shape is an application plus the
properties they think hold, then running it against each level and saying which survive.
That mirrors what a working engineer does when choosing an isolation level, which is the
whole reason this family is worth having.

The oracle is Hermitage. Six rows were checked against PostgreSQL and all agreed.

Three leaks the spike recorded rather than hid. Serialisable modelled as serial is sound
for safety and hides the retry the application owes. Read committed without row locks
cannot express a database-side atomic update. Read uncommitted is where the store and the
committed store come apart, and that is where the mechanism has to return.

title: Curated problem 1: Boyer-Moore majority vote, level 1
description:
The first problem of the curated set, and the first test of whether the shape in
PRACTICE-PLAN.md works at all.

System: the Boyer-Moore majority vote algorithm. tlaplus_Examples at ceeaa90,
specifications/Majority. MIT. Majority.tla is 79 lines with the TLAPS proof isolated in
MajorityProof.tla, so the part that ships stands alone.

Picked over missionaries and cannibals after reading the sources. Missionaries was the
first choice as a calibration anchor, and two facts moved it down the list. Its README
describes the spec rather than the system, so there is no independent description to
check a statement against. And its module is a 225-line tutorial that explains every TLA+
construct it uses in comments, which is an odd artifact to hand over as one example
implementation.

Majority's README is the only one at the low end that actually describes its system.

Frank ruled on 2026-09-05 that familiarity with a domain does not disqualify it, because
the load the scale measures is state representation and knowing an algorithm leaves the
encoding open. He also chose to start at level 1.

Four pieces, and only the first is written from nothing.

- The statement, describing the system and never the spec. No variable named, no data
  structure implied, no decomposition suggested. Note the hazard specific to this one:
  the README names the algorithm's state ("two integer variables and one variable holding
  the current candidate"), so the statement author has to describe the problem the
  algorithm solves without inheriting the solution's shape.
- The choice note, on what the shipped implementation picked that the rules do not force.
- Three to four techniques, read off the implementation, at technique level only.
- The spec, in a subfolder, as one example implementation and never an answer key.

The statement and the other three need opposite inputs. The statement author must not
have the spec open, and the rest can only be written by reading it. Two passes, and the
separation is enforced by what each brief contains rather than by a promise.

Difficulty is assigned after this exists. The level 1 is where the manifest places the
system, not a target.

Four named techniques in notes/TECHNIQUES.md, of which 'Bounding an infinite domain from outside the module' is the state-space technique the ramp has never used in seven problems. title: The manifest finds 24 systems at level 3, the plan says the corpus holds one
description:
PRACTICE-PLAN.md records the level distribution as L1 9, L2 11, L3 1, L4 6, L5 40, and
builds on it. Level 3 holding one system in the whole public corpus is why the plan says
curation covers 1, 2 and 5 while authoring is needed at 3 and 4.

The rebuilt manifest finds 24 systems at level 3 out of 143.

The two counts are not measured over the same set, so this is not yet a contradiction. The
plan counted the 67 that survive describable, fast enough and licence. The manifest counts
every candidate before those filters. Applying them would cut the 24, and by how much is
the question.

I think it needs settling rather than assuming, because a lot rests on it. If level 3 is
genuinely close to empty then the authoring work the plan describes is the main event. If
it holds a dozen usable systems after filtering, then curation reaches further up the
scale than the plan expects and the shape of the next six months changes.

The manifest's why column carries the file:line each level was decided on, so the L3 rows
can be argued with individually rather than re-derived.

So the floor is 5 and the ceiling is 16. Even the floor is five times the plan number.

THE FIVE THAT SURVIVE EVERY FILTER:
  Ledger chaining into a single log            Vanlightly_bookkeeper  MIT  12.6s
  Raft consensus with fsync/durability         Vanlightly_raft        MIT  11.4s
  Non-blocking atomic commitment with FDs      tlaplus_Examples       MIT   5.0s

WHY THIS DOES NOT CHANGE THE DIRECTION, which is the part worth keeping. The bead asks whether a dozen usable level-3 systems would mean curation reaches further up the scale. It would not. Two of the five are consensus or replication, one is atomic commitment, one is a logic puzzle, one is a graph algorithm. Not one is ordinary application engineering. The 2026-09-06 change was made on SHAPE and not on COUNT: tla-frpu says 30 of the 45 usable rows at levels 3 and 4 are consensus, replication, broadcast, leader election or mutual exclusion, and about a dozen rows in 143 look like application engineering. Raising the L3 count from 1 to 5 or even 16 leaves that intact.

THE FILTER CANNOT BE FULLY REPRODUCED, and this is a defect in the manifest rather than in the plan. checkable is unattempted for 92 of 143 rows, 11 of them at level 3. The plan funnel claims 68 of 99 describable systems survived "fast enough to check". The manifest only ran TLC on 51 rows (33 yes, 8 no, 10 timeout). See the TLA_CORPUS path in harness/test-corpus-manifest.sh.

RECOMMENDATION. Correct the funnel table in PRACTICE-PLAN.md to the measured band and record that the count does not carry the direction. Do not spend a TLC pass closing 5-to-16 unless something downstream actually needs the exact number, and I do not see one.

title: The corpus manifest of 67 systems doesn't exist, only its counts
description:
PRACTICE-PLAN.md curates from 67 exercisable public systems. It gives the funnel as 662
modules, 208 specs, 107 distinct systems, 99 describable, 68 fast enough to check, 67
after licence. Levels come out L1 9, L2 11, L3 1, L4 6, L5 40, and prose ships with 50 of
the 67.

None of the rows behind those numbers survived the session that produced them. The palace
holds today's collections survey and today's language-model survey, and neither is the
funnel. Nothing in the repo carries the list. The 16-repo clone that
.claude/rules/tla-practice.md documents is not on disk. So the counts have no artifact
under them, and this is a rebuild rather than a transcription.

That is also the lesson. The manifest lands as a tracked file in the repo, not as a
drawer, because a drawer is what we just lost.

Proposed columns, one row per candidate system. These are the six the funnel's own stages
were computed from, so they hold under any later decision about what a problem entry
carries.

- system, the name we will use
- repo and path, resolvable at a recorded SHA
- licence, read from the repo
- prose, yes or no, and where
- level, 1 to 5 on PRACTICE-PLAN's state-representation scale
- checkable, whether TLC finishes on it, with the wall time

The judgment stages need saying out loud rather than assuming. A module is not a spec, a
spec is not a distinct system, and both boundaries were drawn by hand the first time. The
manifest states each rule next to the count it produces, so the next reader can disagree
with the rule instead of re-deriving it.

Expect the counts to move. I suspect 662 against tla-practice.md's 666 means the two
passes used slightly different repo sets, and I would rather report the drift than
reproduce a number.

title: Six of seven ch11-gated problems need a chapter-12 construct
description:
All seven batch-2 problems declare a chapter-11 reading gate. Six of the seven
references need a chapter-12 construct.

Counted, `EXCEPT` occurrences in each reference: bonded-store 4, river-call 5,
assay-office 4, floor-malting 5, herbarium-sheet 7, estate-notice 4, laytime 0.

The project's own exercise set is what makes this a defect rather than a quibble.
`exercises/ch11/EXERCISES.md` says "Nothing here needs a construct from beyond chapter
11", and `exercises/ch13/EXERCISES.md` says "`EXCEPT` and `@` are chapter 12's". So the
line was drawn deliberately in one place and crossed in another.

It bites two ways. On the shape-A and shape-D rungs the learner writes the spec, and
modeling per-entity state as a function and updating it needs `EXCEPT`, so four
problems cannot be written at their stated gate. On the two shape-B rungs the learner
is HANDED a module containing four `EXCEPT` expressions and told the system half is
not theirs to change, so they read a construct they have not met.

laytime is the one that is genuinely gated right. Zero `EXCEPT`, and its state is
scalar, so it can be modeled with chapter 11 alone. That is luck rather than design,
since nothing in the pipeline checked this.

Frank has finished the first eleven learntla sections and is working laytime now, so
this is live rather than historical.

The same check should run against the gate for tuple subscripts. ch11's exercise set
says a tuple subscript is chapter 12, and every problem asks for a subscript over a
record, which is at least that.

PRACTICE-PLAN.md:166 retires "The load vector and the ramp rule", so the field this bead reads the gate off has no live owner. See tla-t8jz and tla-ahxl.

THAT CUTS THE OTHER WAY, AND IT IS THE USEFUL PART. This bead is the only live CONSUMER of the reading gate I found in an audit of the open P1 queue. title: Two herbarium trades were made to buy things that measure as absent
description:
A NEW category, and the one that bears hardest on whether a model can author this
material. Not a rule reaching too far, and not an invented rule. An author recording
an honest trade whose stated consideration is FALSE about its own artifact.

Two instances, both in herbarium-sheet, both measured.

ONE. Requirement 4 caps a filed slip's stamp at the consultation held, where rule 3's
prose says the slip carries the stamp it came from. Equality in the prose, inequality
in the formula. The author states the trade twice: tighten to equality and
"requirement 1's distinctness clause loses the trace that would isolate it".

That trace does not exist. Measured four ways. Requirement 1's shipped pair breaks the
reading-range clause, not distinctness. No trace in the set holds two slips at one
stamp. Deleting the distinctness conjunct changes no row of 36. And the statement
already tells the learner a forbidden run may break more than one requirement, which
is the objection the cap was kept to avoid. So a weakening was preserved to protect
something that was already absent.

TWO. The commented reference says the fairness measurement gap could be closed by a
bigger instance, and that this would cost the rung its state-space band, so the author
records the limit rather than paying for it. Measured: allowances raised, 105,787
distinct states from 654,135 generated, 408 times the shipped instance, and the
fairness forms still do not separate. A finite cap makes every behaviour finite, so
every fairness form drains the system. No finite instance of this system appears to
separate them. The band was never what was stopping it, and a later author reading
that note will spend a rung's whole state-space budget on a measurement that cannot
come back.

Why this category matters more than the others. Every load-vector finding is the
apparatus deforming a correct model. This is the author being wrong about what its own
artifact does, twice, in writing, with the reasoning laid out honestly. Honest
reasoning from a false premise is not caught by better rules, by a critic, or by a
grader that only ever checks the reference against itself.

Both fixes are small. Tighten requirement 4 to equality. Rewrite the fairness note to
say the discrimination is structurally unavailable rather than priced out.

Found by the taste-critic wave, 2026-09-05.

title: River-call's model was shaped by a file-count rule that does not exist
description:
A NEW failure mode, distinct from the load vector bending the material.

River-call's reference carries instance data in the frozen spec,
`Decrees == [o \in Owners |-> 2]` at `reference/RiverCall.tla:82`. The author knew
it was wrong and said so: "That's a third file, and this rung ships two... If the file
count weren't fixed I'd take the MC module, because instance data in a frozen spec is
a smell" (`author-notes/ALTERNATIVES.md:44-50`).

NO SUCH RULE EXISTS. The nearest thing in the plan is `V2-PLAN.md:1815`, a DELIVERY
LIST: "Deliver: the `.tla`, a `.cfg`, and the named observation operator". A list of
what must be delivered is a floor, not a cap. Measured against the sibling problems:
consign, custody and seedlib each ship an MC module under the same brief, and
seedlib's own notes give the same reason for it.

The cost is a modeling distinction, not just tidiness. Because the register could not
be a third file, an owner's name had to be their priority date
(`reference/RiverCall.tla:4,18`). So seniority rides on identity and nothing in the
model can tell an owner from their place on the register. The author names that loss
at `ALTERNATIVES.md:27-31`.

Why this matters beyond one rung. The load-vector findings are all cases of a REAL
rule reaching too far. This is an author INVENTING a constraint and then paying for
it in the model. Better rules do not fix that. Fewer rules might.

Two options. Ship an MC module for this rung and recover the distinction. Or write
into section 9.4 that the delivery list is a floor, so the next author does not
re-derive the same cap. I would do both, and the second regardless of what happens to
this rung.

title: Observe is a course device and no statement says so
description:
`Observe` is not attested in published TLA+. A 507-module corpus pulled 2026-09-05
carries no property written over a record built from the variables, under any of five
names searched. The three established things it resembles are doing other jobs: VIEW
fingerprints states for the checker in 8 configs, ALIAS formats error traces in 27,
and a refinement mapping projects state but is the target of an implication rather
than the vocabulary requirements are stated in.

The closest published teaching analogue solves the same grading problem the opposite
way. hwayne/tlaplus-exercises fixes both specs and has the learner write only the
property, over the specs' own variable names.

The project has a real reason for the record, at V2-PLAN section 3.3: it is a grading
interface that lets a machine grade without fixing the learner's variable names. That
reason is sound and this bead does not propose dropping it.

What it proposes is saying so. Right now the statements present `Observe` as if it
were how TLA+ is written. The transfer literature is specific about the cost.
Tshukudu 2020 measured true cognates at 2.08 of 3 against false cognates at 0.14 of
3, p under 0.001, and the negative effect persisted where no explicit intervention was
run. Scholtz and Wiedenbeck found that kind of negative transfer hits EXPERIENCED
programmers hardest, which is exactly the audience. Barnett and Ceci put form of
representation among the transfer content least likely to carry.

The literature's remedy is fading, not removal. So: one sentence per statement saying
the record is this course's device and not TLA+ practice, and a rung on the ramp where
it comes off and the learner writes over the spec's own variables.

comments.author: Frank Berthold
comments.text:
2026-09-05, Frank: the record reads as an acquired hangup rather than a decision. Checked, and the shape analysis supports him.

All seven batch-2 problems require properties over Observe. Section 3.3's justification is that it resolves the conflict between never naming the learner's variables and needing a fixed grading interface. That conflict is REAL ON SHAPE A, where the learner writes the spec and their variable names are unknown to the grader.

It does not exist on shape B. authoring/bonded-store/statement/BondedStore.tla:35 hands the learner 'VARIABLES place, dutyPaid' and :2 hands them the constant. The names are fixed by the problem. Observe there is a wrapper around variables the grader already knows, and bonded-store's statement gives no reason for it at all; grep for a justification across all seven statements returns nothing on any shape.

Worse, it is not serving the grading purpose on shape B either. Measured today: bonded-store ships no *RefObl.tla, and grade.sh reads only Req_ operators from a submission, so there is no channel for a learner-authored action property whatever it is written over. So the shape-B learner pays a non-standard notation for a grading path that is not wired.

The one defense worth naming is harness uniformity, one grader and one contract rather than two paths. That cost is hypothetical today because shape B is not gradable, and the learner cost is present.

Scope grows accordingly: this is not one sentence per statement. It is asking whether Observe belongs on shape B at all.

title: The subscript rule is a blanket ban where practice has a coverage rule
description:
Every v2 statement with an action property tells the learner to subscript over the
whole of `Observe`, never one of its fields. That is not the rule practitioners use,
and it is wrong on at least one requirement per problem.

The real condition, stated by Hillel Wayne in TLA+ Action Properties and consistent
with Lamport's own definition `[A]_e == A \/ (e' = e)` where `e` is an expression
rather than a variable: every variable the action mentions must also appear in the
subscript. Corpus check over 507 modules, 676 subscript occurrences: 75 percent a
vars-style tuple, 15 percent an inline tuple, 9 percent a single other name. Four
published specs subscript over a strict projection with the author's reason attached,
including Voting.tla over a derived state function and CosmosDBLinearizability.tla
over a two-element projection of five variables.

Measured on bonded-store, and this is why the blanket rule cannot stand. Requirement
2 mentions only `place`, so a `place` subscript is sound and matches the shipped form
on all 28 modules. Requirement 3 mentions both fields, so the same narrowing there
returns rc=0 on S10 where the full subscript returns rc=13. One rule, two opposite
answers, inside one problem. The blanket ban gets requirement 3 right by accident and
requirement 2 wrong, and it teaches a rule the learner will not find anywhere else.

The coverage rule fixes both without giving away which body is which, because the
learner applies it to whatever they wrote.

Frank raised this working bonded-store as the first real learner, 2026-09-05.

comments.text:
2026-09-05, CORRECTION to this bead's own framing. It said the blanket ban 'gets requirement 3 right by accident and requirement 2 wrong'. That was an isolation artifact and is wrong. The earlier run graded each requirement alone; a learner declares all three. Re-measured with all three declared together: LeavingIsFinal narrowed to _(Observe.place) is identical to the shipped set on all 28 modules. title: grade.sh may be unable to grade any package whose two sides share a CONSTANT
description:
`harness/grade.sh` runs the submission spec against the reference obligations, and
the reference spec against the submission obligations. When a problem carries a
CONSTANT that both sides need, both modules have to declare it, and the judge module
EXTENDs both.

Measured by the tla-nyrb test-author, 2026-09-05: a CONSTANT declared in two EXTENDed
modules is ambiguous. SANY warns, and TLC then reports `the identifier S is either
undefined or not an operator`. Assigning a constant the module does not declare is
silently ignored instead, rc=0. So the vacuity run forces the submission side to
declare it and the chaos run forces the reference obligations to, and there is no
arrangement that satisfies both.

If that holds, the engine cannot grade any package whose problem has a constant both
sides must see. Every batch-2 problem has constants, so this would block grading the
delivered set, not just the pilot. It is also a candidate cause of tla-lt1m.

Central has NOT independently reproduced this. It is one worker's measurement, cited
here as such, and the first job on this bead is to confirm or refute it before
designing anything. The test-author routed around it by collapsing to an empty roster
rather than to a single-member one, which is why the tla-nyrb fixtures do not hit it.

title: An anonymous TLC action suppresses a legitimate grade through the leak gate
description:

title: Research: should model-from-prose (shape A) be half or more of the set, and should its share rise with position?
description:
AUTOFAN-EXCLUDE: research in flight, dispatched by central 2026-09-05 with Frank.

Frank, 2026-09-05, after walking through the six task shapes: his reflex is that as the set proceeds, 50% or more of the problems should be shape A, model from prose. 2.1 settled the allocation at A 18 of 60 (30%), B 8, C 8, D 8, E 6, F 8, plus 4 reserved. He asked for research on whether the didactic approach behind that reflex is right before we change anything.

The question, stated so it can be wrong: for one adult learner acquiring formal modeling (TLA+) through a graded problem set, does a diet dominated by generation tasks (write the model from a system description) produce better modeling ability and transfer than a mixed diet with analysis tasks (write the property given a spec, diagnose a trace, critique a spec)? And does the answer depend on where the learner is on the ramp, so the right A share is a function of position rather than a constant?

Leads the research should test rather than assume. The expertise reversal effect (worked examples help novices, problem solving helps experts) argues for analysis-heavy early and generation-heavy late. Use-modify-create (Lee et al. 2011) and the reading-before-writing results in programming education argue the same shape. The generation effect and productive failure argue for more generation earlier than that. The plan already cites Rohrer 2020 (interleaving), Kornell and Bjork (preference for the format that teaches worst), Cunha et al. ICSE-SEET 2024 (feedback), Greenman et al. and Dyer et al. (properties and traces), Shevrin et al. (example traces), Guindon 1990 (prior schema). Formal-methods-specific evidence (Alloy4Fun corpus studies, LTL misconception work) counts more than general programming-education evidence, which counts more than general learning science, and the report should say which tier each claim sits in.

Output: a findings drawer in tla_puzzles/findings with claims, citations, confidence, and a recommendation on the A share (constant or by position), plus what the seven batch-2 rungs in tla-h2cg.4's draft should do about it. The decision itself is Frank's and lands on tla-h2cg.4 and, if 2.1's allocation moves, on a plan amendment.

title: The sequence script: check the ramp, find an order, or name the hole
description:
Goal: the sequence rule runs as a program over the vector records, so the ramp is gated and not advised, and its output is the order file the practice tree reads.

RED: Given the floor record and the six withdrawn records, When harness/sequence.sh --search runs, Then it reports that no valid order exists and names the first hole as no problem within one new high of the floor. And: Given a synthetic set of records with a known valid order, When --search runs, Then it prints an order in which every neighbour pair satisfies (a), (b), (b') and (c).

The rule, D4 in drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_4cd7acae35ef634cf4ebbabb: (a) no two neighbours share a situation or a task shape. (b) for every dimension, the level at P_i is at most one above the running maximum of that dimension over the floor and P_1 to P_i-1. (b') at most one dimension at P_i is strictly above its running maximum. (c) no problem appears before its reading gate: the sequence carries checkpoints for ch13 and the refinement chapter, and a problem gated on one sits after it. Drops and returns are free.

Two modes. --check <order> verifies a given order and reports the first failing pair and which clause. --search finds an order over all records or reports the hole. Both print where each situation first appears, as information and never as a failure. That line is the nudge Frank weighs, not a gate.

Output is an ORDER file: one problem name per line with the checkpoints inline. Order never lives in a directory name again. Problems are delivered by name under ~/tla-practice/problems/<name>/ and the practice README reads ORDER, so re-placing a problem never touches its directory (tla-oa0m's finding, and Frank's attempts stay put). The README edit overlaps tla-rrwl's hand-in step, so the two don't run in one wave.

The search is over at most 60 items with a monotone constraint, so depth-first with the high-water mark as state is enough. Don't reach for a solver. bash first, python3 if the state bookkeeping gets ugly.

harness/test-sequence.sh carries both RED scenarios. Register in scripts/test. On close, note on tla-kl5.19 that its ordering half is this script.

title: Difficulty progression: the load vector and the ramp rule
description:
Design cycle drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_4cd7acae35ef634cf4ebbabb, locked with Frank 2026-09-04, opened from tla-r6jm.

The v2 set had no difficulty axis. The grid is situation by task shape, the order serves interleaving, and nothing asked whether problem N was reachable from N-1. Two rating passes put all six delivered problems in the upper half of every load column, so no order over them is a ramp. The rungs below them don't exist.

Four decisions. D1: verification is a structural gate, every dimension counted from the artifact, felt difficulty never an input. The one human check is the door test, which is built in because the learner complains anyway. D2: the ramp is an ordering constraint over the sequence, never a third grid axis, so 3.1 stands and the vector is a label. D3: six dimensions, representation, property kind, property count, step sources with time folded in, state space, and form left open, the last one provisional. D4: K=1 against the high-water mark. A dimension may go one level above the highest already reached, and one dimension per problem sets a new high. Drops and returns are free.

Read the drawer before any child. It carries the pinned rubrics, the two invariants, and the two findings drawers, which hold spoilers for every delivered problem.

Children run 1 and 2 in parallel, then 3, 4, 5 in a chain. From the floor, consign needs seven new highs and custody fourteen, so batch 2 is at least seven problems.

title: The problems shipped without the interface a person uses to work them
description:
Frank, 2026-09-04, working problem 00 as the first real learner: "The instructions talk about me handing in results, but with no plan on how to hand them in. These are instructions that are meaningful to a subagent that we're testing the question with, but not actually useful to me, the person they were meant for."

He is right, and the tracker records the inversion.

## The mechanism is specified and its counterparty is unbuilt

`~/tla-practice/README.md` step 4 says "Then ask for the reference. The commented reference and the author's alternatives note get copied into `released/<name>/`, and your attempt gets graded through the harness."

There is nobody to ask. Stage 4 is four beads, all OPEN and none started: `tla-kl5.12` (scaffold the two directories with structural isolation), `tla-kl5.13` (the tutor that does not possess the answer), `tla-kl5.14` (the grader returning a verdict object), `tla-kl5.15` (attempt and impasse logging).

So "ask for the reference" resolves to "ask whatever agent is in your session". That works while somebody who has read the whole design is sitting there, and nothing in the tree says so.

## The dependency was recorded and routed around

`tla-kl5.16`, "Stage 5 section 7 — author batch 1", is blocked on `tla-kl5.13`, `.14` and `.15`. The plan sequenced the tutor before the problems and the edge is in the tracker.

The five delivered problems did not come through that bead. They came through `tla-jjo7`, "Author and deliver problem 1, and let Frank's attempt gate the rest", closed five for five with all eight gates green. That was a deliberate and defensible call on its own terms. Its consequence was not tracked: the artifacts shipped and the interface did not.

## Why no gate caught it, which is the part worth keeping

Every review step in section 6 was run by an agent that was HANDED its artifacts by a dispatcher. The blind solvers never needed a hand-in mechanism because central put the files in front of them and collected the results. The leakage check, the blind-solve spread and both screens all pass without anyone touching the question "can a person operate this".

So the instructions read complete to every reviewer who saw them and are incomplete for their actual audience.

**An agent-run pipeline cannot test the human interface, because the pipeline is the thing standing in for the human.** That is not a missing assertion, it is a blind spot in the shape of the validation, and no amount of care inside section 6 closes it.

## What I would do

Not build all of Stage 4 before Frank can work problem 01. The smallest honest fix is that `PROBLEM.md` and the practice README say what actually happens today: you copy your work into `attempts/<name>/`, you fill the log, and you ask the agent in your session, which is a person-shaped step with no tooling behind it. Written down, that is a workflow. Unwritten, it is a gap the reader has to notice.

Then Stage 4 proper, in the order the plan already gives, with `tla-kl5.16`'s dependency respected rather than routed around.

notes:
PREMISE NOTE 2026-10-01, from the overnight run. The complaint stands. The fix route named in the description is partly dead.

THE COMPLAINT IS UNTOUCHED BY ANY DIRECTION CHANGE. Frank has no way to hand work in. ~/tla-practice/README.md step 4 still says "Then ask for the reference", and there is nobody to ask. That is as true today as on 2026-09-04, and the two problems delivered since (fencing, majority-vote) did not change it.

THE ROUTE IS NOT. The description resolves the gap to four open beads, "tla-kl5.12 (scaffold the two directories with structural isolation), tla-kl5.13 (the tutor that does not possess the answer), tla-kl5.14 (the grader returning a verdict object), tla-kl5.15 (attempt and impasse logging)".

tla-kl5.14 is dead. PRACTICE-PLAN.md:160 retires "The grader and its verdict objects" in those words, and the measurement behind it is in the same file: a model judging a learner work over-validates at 69 to 71 percent over 10,836 solution-feedback pairs (arXiv:2605.16207), and our own blind test agreed, with the holdout going 4 of 5 seeded mutants uncaught and the pilot 5 of 11.

So "your attempt gets graded through the harness" is a promise this project decided not to keep. The README still makes it.

WHAT THAT LEAVES. Three of the four beads survive, and I think they are enough for the actual complaint, which was about handing in rather than about grading. .12 scaffolds the directories, .13 is a language tutor that does not possess the answer, .15 is attempt and impasse logging, which PRACTICE-PLAN.md arguably still wants under a different name (see tla-heql, the reaction log, which has no home and nothing tracked it until today).

So the shape of the fix changes from "hand in and get graded" to "hand in, get the reference, and record your own reaction". That is a smaller build and it drops the component with the measured 69-to-71 percent failure rate.

TWO ADJACENT THINGS THAT BLOCK IT IN PRACTICE:
- tla-bxcd. attempts/ and released/ mirror problems/ by name and that mirror broke when tla-0lwx numbered the directories on 09-18. README step 4 writes into released/<name>/.
- ~/tla-practice/README.md has no source in this repo, so nobody can fix its steps 2 to 4 through a normal commit. Its steps describe a layout that no longer exists.

NOT CLOSING. The route needs rechoosing and that is yours. See the premise audit I left on tla-kl5 for the other children.

title: A delivered chapter can never be repaired, because delivery never overwrites
description:
`scripts/deliver-exercises.sh:37-39` makes never-overwrite absolute: every file is checked for existence first, an existing file is left untouched and reported as "skipped (exists)". That rule is right and it protects the thing that matters most, a half-solved set. It should not be relaxed.

The consequence is that a delivered chapter is frozen at its delivery date. Frank's `~/tla-practice/exercises/ch02` through `ch11` were delivered 2026-08-12 at 22:00. Every repair since then, and every repair after this, reaches the repo and never reaches him.

That is not hypothetical. `tla-e8ps` fixes wording in eight of those ten chapters — sentences telling the learner to read console output the harness deletes. When it closes, Frank's copies will still carry them. He is working ch.09 and ch.10 right now, and both are on that list.

The tension is real rather than a bug: protecting his in-progress work and propagating a fix want opposite behaviours on the same file. I do not think a `--force` flag resolves it, because the file most worth fixing is exactly the file most likely to hold his answers.

What I would build instead is a third state. Delivery already knows whether a file exists; it does not know whether the existing file is his edit or an untouched copy of what was delivered. Recording a digest at delivery time makes that distinguishable:

- unchanged since delivery, and the source has moved → safe to update, do it
- changed since delivery → his work, never touch, report the drift so he can merge by hand
- absent → deliver as now

The reporting half is the part that earns its keep even without the automatic update. Right now nothing tells him a delivered chapter has gone stale, which is the same shape as the three findings from 2026-08-28: a command reports success and does not distinguish "nothing to do" from "something to do that I cannot see".

description:

The printed-command gate is green on ten chapters while twelve exist.

`tla-60le` built this gate precisely so a printed command could not drift from what the delivered tree actually runs. Two chapters outside its list is the drift surface reopening.

The ch.12 author found it, ran the gate out of tree with `CHAPTERS=(12)`, and got 16 assertions all passing. So the fix is likely just the array. It was left alone deliberately: the array sits outside both exercise beads' `Files:` lines and the two authors would have collided on it.

Fix: add `12` and `13`. Then consider whether the list should be derived rather than written. A gate whose coverage is a hand-maintained list has the same failure mode as the pin that started this: it is correct until somebody adds a chapter and forgets. Deriving it from the directories under `exercises/` that carry an `EXERCISES.md` would close it for good, and that is the version I would rather ship.
