title: The recall miss counts are hand-written in about twenty places and gated in two
description:
Adding one MISS row for R024 (tla-n001) required editing eight sites that
restate a number the corpus already knows. One of them is an assertion and
would have gone red. The other seven are prose and would have gone quietly
wrong.

THE SITES, from a grep for the two phrasings over *.md, *.tsv and *.sh:

  recall/MISSES.tsv:4          91 rows, 31 over 31 ...      prose, header
  recall/MISSES.tsv:50         90 of the 120 REP rows       prose
  recall/MISSES.tsv:60         30 of the 120 REP rows do    prose
  recall/README.md:695         91 rows: 31 over 31 ...      prose
  recall/README.md:446         90 of the 120 reps           prose
  recall/recall.sh:1739        90 of the 120 reps           comment
  harness/test-recall-runner.sh:31, 1119, 1164  90 of 120   comments
  harness/fixtures/recall/MISSES.tsv:30         90 of 120   comment
  harness/test-recall-gate.sh:718               91 miss row ASSERTION

Only the last one gates. It is also the only one that caught the change.

WHY THIS IS THE SAME SHAPE WE ALREADY NAMED. .claude/rules/dispatched-agents.md
says a hardcoded suite count in prose goes stale and records two occasions it
did, which is why that file now points at `bash scripts/test --list` as the
authority instead of carrying a number. The miss counts have the same problem
and no authority to point at.

I also wrote a wrong mutant count into scripts/test on 2026-10-16 and corrected
it on 2026-10-17 at 856b644. Three instances now.

WHAT I WOULD BUILD. One assertion that derives the counts from the two tables
and compares them against what the prose claims, so the prose can stay and
cannot drift. The derivation is cheap and needs no TLC:

  rows            grep -c '^MISS' recall/MISSES.tsv
  REP with a row  grep '^MISS' MISSES.tsv | cut -f2 | grep '^R' | sort -u | wc -l
  REP with none   120 minus the above

The harder half is that the prose spells the same number six different ways,
so an assertion has to find them. I think the answer is to pick one phrasing
per number and gate on that exact string, the way part 16 of the runner suite
pins an exact column string, rather than trying to parse English.

THE ALTERNATIVE WORTH NAMING. Delete the counts from the five comment sites
and keep them only in the two table headers plus the assertion. That is less
work and loses something real, since the comments use the number to say why a
code path matters ("the path 90 of the 120 real reps take"). I would keep them
and gate them.

title: R024's implication has a constant consequent, so it collapses into a negated-equality rep
description:
Frank, 2026-10-17, working R024 in the delivered tree: "this next one feels
incoherent." He read it as `Parking["c"] = 3 => ("c" = "b")`, which is the
canonical answer, and then said it is equivalent to `Parking["c"] # 3`. Both
readings are right.

    REP  R024  K009  shunting
    whether wagon c being on the third track would mean that wagon c is wagon b
    Parking.c = 3 => "c" = "b"

## What is wrong with it

The consequent compares two string literals. It does not read the environment,
so it is a constant, and the whole implication is `TRUE => FALSE`.

Verified against recall/env/shunting.tla:

    R024 as written              FALSE
    Parking.c # 3                FALSE      (Frank's reduction, same value)
    R023, Parking.b = 3 => ...   TRUE

So the rep that is supposed to exercise `=>` is extensionally `Parking.c # 3`,
which is the shape of R010, a K003 rep. A learner who sees the collapse writes
the K003 answer and is graded correct on an implication rep.

## It is the only one

Scanned field 6 of all 120 REP rows for a comparison with a literal on both
sides. R024 is the single hit. Every other K009 consequent reads something:

    R023  Parking.b = 3 => Parking.c = 3                     model state
    R025  Train[1] = "a" => Cardinality(Wagons) = 4          model state
    R026  \A acct \in Accounts : Balance[acct] = 0 => acct = "bo"   bound variable

R026 is the one to compare against, because its consequent also compares to a
literal. The difference is that `acct` is bound by the quantifier, so the
comparison is a real question. R024's `"c"` is not bound by anything.

## Why the English reads as nonsense

A prompt has to describe what the expression computes. When the expression
compares two names, the only English available is "wagon c is wagon b", which
is a category error in the model's own terms: wagons are the strings a, b and
c, and asking whether one name is another name is not a question about a yard.
The incoherence in the prose is downstream of the degeneracy in the formula,
not a separate wording problem.

## The slot is worth keeping

The four K009 reps cover true antecedent with true consequent (R023), vacuous
truth (R025), quantified implication (R026), and R024 is the true antecedent
with a false consequent. That is a real case and the set is poorer without it.
It just needs a non-degenerate instance.

What I would write, the exact mirror of R023 on the same record:

    whether wagon c being on the third track would mean wagon a is on it too
    Parking.c = 3 => Parking.a = 3

Verified FALSE against shunting.tla, so it fills the same slot, and both sides
read the environment. R023 and this then form a true/false pair over one
record, which is a better demonstration of implication than either alone.

## Nothing records what goes wrong here

MISSES.tsv has 0 rows for R024, and 0 for R023 and R026. Only R025 of the four
implication reps carries a miss. So the family with the subtlest semantics has
one recorded misconception across four reps.

Files: recall/REPS.tsv, recall/MISSES.tsv
notes:
2026-10-17, central. Measured the rest of the K009 family before authoring
miss rows, and found the bigger defect. Two corrections and one new finding.

CORRECTION 1. I told Frank the implication family's miss coverage was
unusually thin. It is the median. Coverage per construct across all 120 REP
rows: 12 of 37 constructs have no miss at all, 20 have exactly one, 5 have
two. K009 at 1 of 4 rows is the ordinary case, and the header of MISSES.tsv
already states the design, 30 miss rows over 30 of the 120 rows. There is no
K009-specific coverage gap.

CORRECTION 2. R023 resists a miss row for a reason, and the reason is the
real defect.

THE FINDING. Two of the four implication reps can be answered with a
conjunction and are graded correct. Measured through recall.sh, not by
reading:

  R023, answered Parking.b = 3 /\ Parking.c = 3   rc=0 token=OK correct
  R023, answered Parking.b = 3 <=> Parking.c = 3  rc=0 token=OK correct

The first of those is R018's canonical answer verbatim, a K007 rep. So the
same string is the right answer to a conjunction rep and to an implication
rep.

THE MECHANISM. For atoms P and Q, P => Q and P /\ Q differ exactly when P is
false. A rep whose antecedent is true cannot tell implication from
conjunction. Values on shunting and ledger:

  rep                       canonical   same rep as /\   discriminates
  R023  true antecedent     TRUE        TRUE             no
  R024  true antecedent     FALSE       FALSE            no
  R025  false antecedent    TRUE        FALSE            yes
  R026  false for ann       TRUE        FALSE            yes

So R025 and R026 earn their place and R023 and R024 do not require the
construct they are filed under.

WHAT THIS DOES TO THE PROPOSED REPLACEMENT. The row I proposed above,
Parking.c = 3 => Parking.a = 3, is still right for coherence and still fills
the true-antecedent-false-consequent slot. It does NOT fix discrimination:
measured FALSE, and the conjunction form is also FALSE. That slot is the one
case where an implication is false, and conjunction agrees with implication
there by construction, so no choice of atoms fixes it.

THE FIX ALREADY EXISTS AND IS UNADOPTED. Field 7, built and gated in the
fixture by tla-1sh7.5, holds an ERE matched against the raw answer and
refuses with rc 4 CONSTRUCT_NOT_WRITTEN. tla-1sh7.7 adopts it for the seven
definition forms, K001 and K071 to K076, for exactly this reason: value
equality cannot see that a construct was written. The implication rows need
the same thing and are not in that bead's scope. Noted on tla-1sh7.7.

SCOPE OF WHAT I MEASURED. K009 only, four rows, by evaluating each canonical
and its conjunction form against both environments and then confirming the
two that matter through the runner. I did not scan the other 36 constructs
for the same shape, and K007's or/and rows are the obvious place it would
also live.
close_reason: Merged at 075ce24, implemented at 69fb1b2. R024's consequent compared two string literals, so it never read the environment, the rep was extensionally Parking.c # 3, and a learner could answer an implication rep with the K003 construct and grade correct. The replacement mirrors R023 on the same record, Parking.c = 3 => Parking.a = 3, which keeps the true-antecedent-false-consequent slot the K009 family needs. Measured through recall.sh: canonical rc 0, converse rc 10. Scanned field 6 of all 120 REP rows and R024 was the only comparison with a literal on both sides. Gates green: recall corpus gate 188 passed, recall runner 402 passed, lint clean over 82 files. Two things deliberately left: the row still cannot tell => from /\ because those agree wherever the antecedent is true, which is tla-1sh7.7's field 7, and the miss row the converse earns is blocked on tla-z4f3.

title: The two recall environments disagree on record notation, and the report shows it as if it were the error
description:
On R018 Frank typed bracket notation and the canonical answer came back in dot
notation:

    you typed   Parking["a"] = 3 /\ Parking["c"] = 3
    the answer  Parking.b = 3 /\ Parking.c = 3

His actual error is one character, a where the prompt said b. The display
changes two things at once, and the notation change is the one that scans.

## The grader is not at fault

Both notations grade correct, verified in both directions:

    Parking["b"] = 3 /\ Parking["c"] = 3  on R018  -> rc=0 token=OK correct
    Balance.ann # Balance.bo              on R009  -> rc=0 token=OK correct

Grading is value equality, so this never was a correctness question.

## The corpus is split by environment

Counting canonical answers that access a record at a LITERAL key, where both
notations are legal and the author chose:

    shunting   9 rows dot      R007 R010 R018 R019 R020 R023 R024 R028 (+1)
    ledger     5 rows bracket  R009 R013 R022 R029 R046

The remaining bracket uses are forced rather than chosen: EXCEPT requires it
(R114 R116 R117 R118 R119 R120) and so does a variable key (R032's
Parking[w]). So the free choice went one way in one environment and the other
way in the other, for the same operation.

## Two separable questions

1. Should the corpus pick one notation for a literal key? I would say yes, and
   I do not have a view on which, since both are ordinary TLA+ and a learner
   meets both. Worth noting that teaching only one leaves the other unread.

2. Should the report point at the difference it found? That is the half that
   bit here and it is independent of question 1. Two expressions are printed
   next to each other and the reader does the diff. On a one-character error
   inside a notation change, that is the whole failure.

I think 2 is the one worth building and 1 is a judgment call that can wait.

Files: recall/REPS.tsv, recall/recall.sh, harness/test-recall-runner.sh

title: A retry re-prints the whole battery, which scrolls the reader's own error off the screen
description:
Found by central on 2026-10-17, running the delivered tree right after tla-1sh7.12 and tla-1sh7.13 landed at 169d53a. Both fixes work. They interact badly on one row kind.

MEASURED, in ~/tla-practice/recall, seed 7, which serves S025 and its three machines:

  prompt + scope block   46 lines
  answer, error, caret, two sentences   8 lines
  then the whole 46 lines again

So on a retry the reader's own typo, the caret under it and SANY's sentence sit 46 lines above the new prompt. On a 24-line terminal they are gone before the reader can act on them, and the retry exists precisely so they can act on them.

The two fixes are each right on their own. The block belongs under a prompt a reader is seeing for the first time. On the SECOND go the reader read it eight lines ago, and what they need on screen is the error.

SIZE IS THE WHOLE OF IT, and it is a spec-row problem rather than a session problem. A REP row's block is five lines, so a retry there costs six and the error stays on screen: verified on R119, Frank's own row, where the typo, the caret and the corrected answer all fit in 32 lines. 20 of the 40 SPEC rows name more than one scaffold, and a three-machine row like S025 is 45 lines of block.

OPTIONS, none of them measured yet, and whoever takes this should run them rather than pick one here:

  1  On a retry print the prompt alone, since the block has not changed and
     the reader just read it. Cheapest, and it keeps the error adjacent.
  2  On a retry print the block only for the machine SANY named, which the
     runner already knows: ANSWER_LINE comes from SPEC_FIRST_BAD.
  3  Re-print the error UNDER the new prompt rather than above it.

I would try 1 first and look at 2 only if a reader says they lost the machine.

NOT A REGRESSION IN EITHER BEAD. Before them a parse error spent the rep, so there was no second prompt to scroll anything off. This is a defect the retry created and the battery sizes.

RED: INVARIANT: on a parse-error retry the message that explains the parse error is still on a 24-line screen when the reader types the next answer, on a three-scaffold SPEC row as well as on a REP row.

Files: recall/recall.sh, recall/README.md, harness/test-recall-runner.sh

Fixed at 72a1b22, merged at ea9de77. Option 1 as Frank ruled: on a retry the session prints the prompt alone, one rule for both row kinds with no size threshold.

  fixture R004, a value row      16 -> 13, never crossed 24

The guard is one clause: [ "$QUIET" = "0" ] && [ "$tries" = "1" ] && session_scope ... at recall/recall.sh:1201.

Suite 393 -> 402 assertions, 89.4s standalone (was 86.8), so the 88.6 budget needs re-basing from the next in-suite reading. M16 deletes the new clause and leaves the line, controlled on the span: 40 against 13. M14's pattern was re-anchored for the reason M1 and M2 were, since it matched the QUIET test alone and a second test went beside it.

title: Second slice: pluscal, 31 constructs
description: The largest family and affordable at 1.27x, because pcal.trans costs 90 to 130 ms rather than a second JVM. Three things gate it, all measured in tla-1sh7.9. An unbounded wrong answer returned 124 TIMEOUT after 60.3s, so every rep ships a type invariant capping the state space and the runner passes a short budget. --fair algorithm plus PROPERTY Termination is what catches a non-progressing answer. And pcal.trans exits 255 on a syntax error, colliding with TLC_EXCEPTION in verdict.sh's table, so a translation failure reports as 99 CHECK_DID_NOT_RUN. Roughly 7 of the 31 ask what the translation produces and belong on the value-equality rung instead, with the translated module as the environment. Files: recall/, harness/recall-gate.sh

title: Split harness/test-deliver-recall.sh out of the recall gate suite
description: Every sibling delivery script has a suite named after it: test-deliver-drill.sh, test-deliver-completion.sh, test-deliver-problems.sh, test-deliver-exercises.sh. scripts/deliver-recall.sh has none. The tla-1sh7.4 worker put its coverage in harness/test-recall-gate.sh part 6 and labelled it with the reason rather than shipping the script ungated, because an ungated delivery script is the shape that deleted 39 files on 2026-10-02. Splitting it out is the follow-up. Read part 6 first: the claim it measures rather than asserts is that no file in the recall channel is learner-owned, so the whole manifest is always overwritten, which inverts the siblings' never-overwrite rule. That inversion is the thing a dedicated suite most needs to keep honest, because the day a learner-owned file appears in recall/ is the day always-overwrite destroys work. title: Deliver the three drill-root reference files, and invert the two assertions that forbid it
description:
Decide about all three drill-root reference files together, and deliver them.

drill/SHEET.md, drill/INVENTORY.md and drill/COLD-LIST.md all sit in the repo
and none reaches the practice tree. harness/test-deliver-drill.sh:937-938
asserts two of them never do:

  assert_absent "drill/INVENTORY.md is not an item and never lands" ...
  assert_absent "drill/COLD-LIST.md is not an item and never lands" ...

Those assertions were right when an item was the only thing a delivery
carried. They are not a ruling about reference material, which did not exist
then.

WHY IT IS ONE DECISION AND NOT THREE. The cold list says what you cannot
write from a blank page. The sheet gives the shape of what you could not
write. The inventory says which items reach it. drill/README.md:71-76 has a
"## The construct list" section pointing at COLD-LIST.md that never mentions
the sheet, so the delivered README already describes half an answer.

WHERE IT GOES. scripts/deliver-drill.sh, not deliver-recall.sh. The tla-1sh7.4
worker's reasoning, and I agree: the delivered recall runner already looks for
$HOME/tla-practice/drill/SHEET.md, which is exactly where deliver-drill.sh
puts the drill corpus, so the path lines up with no flag. Delivering it from
the recall script would put two scripts in charge of one destination
directory.

THE SHAPE TO COPY IS ALREADY THERE. drill/README.md is a repo-owned
always-overwrite class in that same script, for the reason the header gives:
the repo is the source of truth for it and Frank never edits it. All three
reference files are in that class.

A missing sheet is silence rather than a refusal, so reps still grade without
it. This is not a blocker for the channel, which is why it is P2 and separate
from the verdict.sh bug.

RED: INVARIANT: a drill delivery lands drill/SHEET.md, drill/INVENTORY.md and drill/COLD-LIST.md at the practice tree's drill root, always overwriting, and harness/test-deliver-drill.sh asserts each one lands rather than asserting two never do.

title: Adopt field 7 in the live reps so the definition forms and the implication rows gate their construct
description:
Adopt field 7 in recall/REPS.tsv, so the definition rows gate the construct
rather than only drilling it.

tla-1sh7.5 built the mechanism and gated it in the fixture. A seventh TSV
field holds an ERE matched against the raw answer, refusal is rc 4
CONSTRUCT_NOT_WRITTEN, and a six-field row behaves exactly as before. None of
the 120 live rows uses it yet.

WHO NEEDS IT. The seven definition forms, K001 and K071 to K076. They grade
rc 0 wrapped in a LET, so they drill the construct, but value equality cannot
see that a definition was written and a learner who computes the same value
another way passes. tla-1sh7.2 measured that and said so.

ADOPTION NEEDS NOTHING ELSE. The tla-1sh7.5 worker searched every consumer of
REPS.tsv: four files, and the only one outside its own footprint is
scripts/gen-misses.sh, which reads with awk -F'\t' and cut and carries zero
NF references, so a seventh field does not reach it. The field-count
assumption lived only in harness/test-recall-runner.sh and now accepts 6 or 7.

THE TRAP, MEASURED, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE JOB. A pattern strict enough to
require the construct must still accept every correct way of writing it.
Against \bLET\b on the fixture: a renamed operator scores 0, a changed body
scores 0, and a whole function defined rather than the element scores 0,
while the form with no LET scores 4. A tighter pattern anchored on the
operator's own spelling, ^LET [A-Za-z]+\(t\) ==, would have refused two of
those three correct answers.

So for every pattern you add, write at least three correct alternates and
measure each. Put the measurements in your report. A pattern with one
alternate behind it is a pattern nobody tested.

K008, bullet-point boolean notation, still has no rep at all. The gate it was
waiting on now exists, but the other half of its problem does not move: a
tab-delimited row is one line and the construct is a layout made of line
breaks. Decide that separately and do not let it block the seven.

RED: INVARIANT: every definition-form rep in recall/REPS.tsv carries a field-7 pattern; each pattern scores 4 against an answer that reaches the right value without the construct, and 0 against at least three correct alternates that spell it differently.

Files: recall/REPS.tsv
notes:
2026-10-17, central. A second family needs field 7, found while working
tla-n001. The bead's scope line says the seven definition forms, K001 and
K071 to K076. The implication rows have the same defect for the same reason.

MEASURED through recall.sh:

  R023, answered Parking.b = 3 /\ Parking.c = 3   rc=0 token=OK correct
  R023, answered Parking.b = 3 <=> Parking.c = 3  rc=0 token=OK correct

R023's canonical is Parking.b = 3 => Parking.c = 3. The conjunction that
passes is R018's canonical answer verbatim, a K007 rep, so one string is the
right answer to a rep about /\ and to a rep about =>.

WHY. P => Q and P /\ Q differ exactly when P is false, so an implication rep
with a true antecedent cannot require implication. Of the four K009 rows,
R023 and R024 have true antecedents and do not discriminate. R025 and R026 do.

This is the same sentence as the bead's own rationale, "value equality cannot
see that a definition was written and a learner who computes the same value
another way passes", with definition replaced by implication.

A PATTERN FOR THESE IS EASIER THAN FOR THE DEFINITION FORMS. The construct is
a single operator rather than a layout, so the trap the bead describes, a
pattern strict enough to require the construct while accepting every correct
spelling, is a narrower problem here. The alternates to measure are the ones
that reach the same value with the operator present, for instance a different
but equivalent arrangement of the two sides, and the refusal case is the bare
conjunction. The bead's rule still applies: three correct alternates per
pattern, each measured, in the report.

NOT SCANNED. Only K009, four rows. K007's and/or rows are the next place to
look, since a disjunction over two true operands has the same shape, and I
did not measure them.

Whether to widen this bead or file the implication rows separately is Frank's
call. They are the same mechanism and the same file, which argues for one
bead.
2026-10-17, Frank: widen this bead to cover the implication rows rather than
filing them separately. Same mechanism, same file.

SCOPE AS IT NOW STANDS, superseding the "WHO NEEDS IT" paragraph above:

  the seven definition forms  K001, K071 to K076   7 rows
  the implication rows        K009                 4 rows

The two halves need the same proof and the same care, so the bead's existing
rule holds for both: every pattern gets at least three correct alternates
that spell the construct differently, each measured, with the measurements in
the report. A pattern with one alternate behind it is a pattern nobody tested.

The refusal case differs between the halves. For a definition form it is an
answer that reaches the value without a LET. For an implication row it is the
bare conjunction, which is what passes today:

  R023, answered Parking.b = 3 /\ Parking.c = 3   rc=0 token=OK correct

R025 and R026 already discriminate on value alone, so a pattern there buys
less. Add it anyway for uniformity across the family, or say in the report why
not. Either is defensible and the choice should be stated rather than left to
whoever reads the rows later.

ORDER. tla-n001 replaces R024's row in the same file. Land that first so this
bead is not writing a field 7 pattern onto a row that is about to change.
close_reason: Merged at 87aa35b (merge commit on main). 24 of 120 reps carry a field-7 ERE, up from 0. Scope corrected: the bead said 11 rows and the real figure is 24, because the seven definition CONSTRUCTS cover fifteen rows and K007 was never scanned and leaks on all five of its rows. Measured 24 canonicals at rc 0, 90 correct alternates at rc 0, 58 refusals at rc 4, every alternate first verified against the unpatched table. A SANY probe set the alphabet rather than taste: \land \lor \lnot \neg all parse so an ASCII-only pattern would refuse a correct answer, \equiv parses and reaches R023's value so it is a refusal case, and \implies is rc 150. Corrects the bead on R025 and R026, which accept the material-implication rewrite and a bare TRUE, so a pattern there closes a real leak rather than buying uniformity. Fields 1 to 6 moved on no line. 12 new runner assertions covering the three ERE shapes the fixture never exercised, with the first construct-gate mutant that file has had. Filed tla-2s12 for the rot surface it measured: check 4 cannot see a MISSING pattern, so the adoption is ungated.

title: Record the > versus >> truncation hazard, and fix gen-coverage.sh's silent --root exit
description:
Two awk or sed passes writing > to one file truncate each other, and the
dispatched-agents hazard list does not name it.

MEASURED 2026-10-16 by the tla-ucbs worker with a fixture rather than
inferred: two runs redirecting > to one path leave only SECOND, two runs with
>> leave both. It cost that worker a real finding. Its first run detected
exercises/templates/CHEATSHEET.md as an untracked thirteenth cheat sheet,
wrote the BADCHAPTER line, and the second pass silently ate it. The worker
only recovered the finding because it re-ran.

WHY IT BELONGS IN THE RULES FILE. .claude/rules/dispatched-agents.md already
carries the two hazards of this exact family: the ugrep wrapper that returns
the wrong count, and the pipefail SIGPIPE that reports a present pattern as
absent. Both are silent-wrong-answer shapes, and both are in the file because
somebody lost work to them first. This is the third, and it is the one most
likely to hit a worker that fans a generator out over several passes, which is
the shape this project's generators keep taking.

WHAT TO WRITE. Short, next to the other two. The hazard is a multi-pass
generator where each pass appends findings to a report or an output file. The
fix is >> everywhere, plus a gate: a static count of > against >> in the
generator, and a fixture requiring one output from each pass in a single run.
The tla-ucbs worker gated it both ways in harness/test-sheet.sh, so that file
is the worked example to cite.

A SECOND, SMALLER ITEM FROM THE SAME WORKER, worth a line in the same pass.
A --root style flag with no value exits 1 silently, because the trailing
shift dies under set -e before the guard that would report the missing value.
It fixed this in scripts/gen-sheet.sh and found the same bug live in
scripts/gen-coverage.sh on --inventory, --drill and --reading:
scripts/gen-coverage.sh --inventory exits 1 today with no message. That is a
generator this project's gate depends on.

title: Recall: the misconception table from the verify comments
description:
Build the misconception table: a wrong answer maps to an explanation of what
it actually says.

DEPENDS ON the rep table, which supplies the rep ids this keys against.

THE SOURCE IS ALREADY WRITTEN. 406 of the 498 modules under drill/*/*/verify/
carry a leading comment naming one specific wrong move and its consequence,
each with a measured rc recorded in the item's ANSWER.md and re-verified by
drill-gate.sh CHECK 2 on every gate pass. Two examples, both from
functions-records/01-shunting-yard:

  ShuntYardLiteralEq: "Init says pos EQUALS a function literal. pos is then
  one function, and its value at every wagon is the whole set Tracks rather
  than a track."

  ShuntYardLiteralInit: "Init asks whether pos is IN a function literal. The
  right-hand side is one function, wagon to the set Tracks, and membership in
  a function is not a thing TLC can evaluate."

Those are construct-level explanations wearing a module's variable name. The
work is re-keying them from item to construct and rewriting each to name no
module.

WHAT TO BUILD. recall/MISSES.tsv, tab-delimited with a literal first field
MISS. Fields: marker, rep id, the wrong answer verbatim, the explanation.
scripts/gen-misses.sh is the harvesting aid, not the authority: it extracts
candidate comments by construct for a human pass. The file is authored, not
generated, because the rewrite from "pos" to no-module prose is a judgment.

THE EXPLANATION SAYS WHAT THE WRONG ANSWER IS, NOT WHAT TO DO INSTEAD. "You
wrote one function whose value at each element is the whole set" is the
register. "You need a function set" is not, because the dual value block in
the runner is already showing the right answer and the sheet entry is already
naming it. This layer exists to explain the mistake.

A MISS ROW IS NOT REQUIRED. A rep with no recorded misses falls through to the
model call, which is layer 4 and is safe at this rung because the answer is
already on screen. Do not pad the file to reach coverage.

HAZARDS. Never field-split a TSV with IFS=$'\t' read. The wrong answers
contain TLA+, so write the file with the Write tool rather than a shell
heredoc. Do not edit anything under drill/*/*/verify/.

RED: INVARIANT: every wrong answer in recall/MISSES.tsv scores rc 10 through recall/recall.sh against its own rep id, and no explanation names a module or a variable from the verify tree.

Files: recall/MISSES.tsv, scripts/gen-misses.sh
close_reason: Merged at 4bc0736 (worker commit 56e97e3). recall/MISSES.tsv is 30 rows over 25 of the 37 constructs, plus scripts/gen-misses.sh as the harvesting aid with a --todo mode. Central re-ran every row through the runner independently: rc10=30, other=0, every row four fields. Read a sample and the register is right: each explanation says what the wrong answer MEANS rather than naming the fix. 'That is a set, so it holds no order and reads the same written the other way round. Which wagon stands at the front is gone.' DELIBERATELY NOT PADDED: 90 of 120 reps carry no row and fall through to the model call, which is layer 4 by design. The twelve constructs with no row carry a reason each at the foot of the file, in three groups: five where the corpus's own recorded mistakes come back rc 150 and so report on the text rather than on a misconception, two where value equality cannot see a name was introduced, five where no mistake in the drill corpus would be caught by these reps. 45 candidates measured, 44 at rc 10, one dropped at 150. Two gate findings appended to tla-1sh7.4: a whole-word match against declared verify-tree names fires on the English words a, at, where, holds, taken and occupied; and an evaluation failure inside the ASSUME surfaces as rc 10 rather than a separate code, so that band holds both a wrong value and no value at all.

title: A worker's injected project instructions are a snapshot, so a mid-session fix is invisible to it
description:
Files: .claude/rules/dispatched-agents.md

REPORTED TWICE ON 2026-10-15, by the tla-d6o0.4 and tla-3rmn authors, hours
apart and independently.

Both reported that `.claude/rules/dispatched-agents.md` says "28 suites, ~357 s"
and an "18-suite, ~26 s tier". Both were right about what they read and wrong
about the file. I removed those numbers at 1ff0c69 earlier the same session,
and `command grep -nE '28 suites|18-suite'` over the file on disk returns
nothing.

WHAT THEY READ WAS THE INJECTED COPY. Project instructions arrive in a
worker's context as a system reminder built when its session starts, and that
snapshot does not refresh when the file on disk changes. The tla-d6o0.4 author
said so explicitly: "the system-reminder copy still records as 28 suites".

SO A MID-SESSION FIX TO ANY PROJECT INSTRUCTION FILE IS INVISIBLE to every
worker already running, and to workers dispatched afterwards if the injection
is cached per project rather than per dispatch. Which of those two it is was
not established and is worth measuring, because it decides whether a fix
reaches the next wave or only the next session.

TWO CONSEQUENCES WORTH ACTING ON.

A correction I make to a rules file during a wave does not reach that wave. If
the correction matters to work in flight, it has to go in a SendMessage to the
running workers as well, which is what I did for the EXTENDS hazard tonight
and did not do for this one.

A worker reporting a discrepancy against its injected instructions may be
reading a stale copy rather than finding a real defect. Both of tonight's
reports were correct observations and wrong conclusions, and both were marked
as discrepancies, which is the right handling. The brief should tell them to
re-read the file from disk before reporting one, and that one line in the
rules file would have saved two reports.

THE IRONY WORTH RECORDING. The number they flagged is the one the file's own
paragraph predicts will go stale, and it had gone stale three times before.
The fourth report was about a copy rather than the file, which is a fifth way
for a hardcoded count to mislead.

title: sequences/01-triage-board needs a guard-bounded neighbour before its telegraph can be cut
description:
Files: drill/sequences/01-triage-board/PROMPT.md, drill/sequences/01-triage-board/verify/

AUDIT-telegraph.md judges this FAIL-mild, and it is the item central
deliberately held back from the 2026-10-14 fixes so the audit would have it
rather than a third one-off edit.

The sentence: the prompt closes "Say how you stopped the treated list growing
without bound". That tells the reader the treated list grows without bound,
which IS the CONSTRAINT lesson, before they have run anything.

WHY IT CANNOT BE FIXED THE USUAL WAY. The remedy pattern is cut the hint,
state the model, publish the count, and let the count do the foreclosing. That
needs a wrong-but-clean neighbour in verify/ with a DIFFERENT count. The audit
checked and there is none: `TriageSelect` is clean at the same 7225 and is
caught by its Admits run instead. So publishing 7225 forecloses nothing.

WHAT THIS BEAD IS. Measure a guard-bounded neighbour, one that runs clean and
lands on a count other than 7225, so that publishing the figure actually rules
the wrong model out. Then cut the sentence and publish the count.

If no such neighbour can be built, say so and leave the sentence. The audit is
explicit that removing a reader's only foothold is worse than the leak, and
the authors kept these on purpose.

title: A TLA+ parse error whose text contains a percent sign reports as a Java format exception
description:
Files: .claude/rules/tla-practice.md (a line in the toolchain notes), optional

MEASURED 2026-10-15 by the tla-d6o0.6 author, on TLC2 Version
2026.07.31.184830 (rev 30cc360), this project's pinned v1.8.0 build.

A parse error whose offending text contains `%` destroys its own diagnostic.
The message comes back as:

  java.util.UnknownFormatConversionException: Conversion = 'i'

and names NEITHER the line NOR the cause. Reproduced under both `tlc` and
`java -cp tla2tools.jar tla2sany.SANY`, so it is in SANY rather than in the
wrapper.

DISCRIMINATED RATHER THAN ASSUMED. A syntax error with no `%` in it, `Foo ==
5 + 3 ) 1`, prints a normal `***Parse Error***` with a line and a column. The
minimal failing case is a four-line module containing `Foo == 5 % 3 + 1`.

WHY THAT EXPRESSION IS A PARSE ERROR AT ALL, which is the useful half for a
reader: TLA+ gives `%` precedence 10-11 and `+` precedence 10-10, so mixing
them unparenthesized is a precedence conflict rather than an arithmetic
question. `(5 % 3) + 1` parses. This is a real trap for anyone writing modular
arithmetic, which is most recurrences.

HOW IT COST A RUN. PLAN-reading-expansion.md:325 predicted rc 12 from a
mutation written as `J(n - 1) % n + 1`. The real result is PARSE_ERROR rc 150
with the Java exception above, so the predicted failure was unreachable from
that mutation AND the error said nothing about why. Parenthesized as the plan
meant it, the probe gives rc 12 as predicted, though at a different parameter.

WORTH RECORDING WHERE SOMEONE WILL SEE IT. The exit-code table in
drill/study/check's header already carries five measured rc classes and would
take a sixth line. .claude/rules/tla-practice.md is the other candidate, under
a toolchain note. Either is better than leaving the next person to rediscover
that `%` in a broken expression hides the breakage.

NOT WORTH REPORTING UPSTREAM FROM HERE without checking it against a current
nightly first. The build is from July and the project pins it deliberately
(bead tla-wl7), so the bug may already be fixed in tlaplus HEAD.

title: The study config does not know about config= or a NOT RUN: line
description:
Files: drill/study/CLAUDE.md, drill/study/.claude/commands/check.md

Raised by the tla-rzvk.4 worker as outside its own two files, and it is right.

tla-rzvk.4 added two things to the checker's output that no guidance covers:

  module=pickers_collision config=pickers.cfg rc=12 ... run=VIOLATED invariant=NoDoublePicks
  module=<name> NOT RUN: no <name>.cfg, and 2 configs to choose from: A.cfg, B.cfg

Nothing in the study config is now FALSE. check.md:21 says to quote the
checker's numbers as printed, which still holds, and neither file ever quoted
the line format. So this is a gap rather than a defect.

The gap is that a session seeing `config=pickers.cfg` on `module=pickers_
collision` has nothing telling it the config was BORROWED rather than written
for that module, and a `NOT RUN:` line arrives with no guidance at all.

What the guidance should say, in the existing behavior-not-construct register:

  - A borrowed config is normal and not a finding. Frank runs two models off
    one config on purpose when both declare the same constants and rules.
  - A borrowed config IS worth a word when the two modules disagree about
    what they need, because then the run checked something other than what
    the module means.
  - A NOT RUN: line means no verdict exists for that module, which is not the
    same as a clean one. Say so rather than letting the absence read as a pass.
    This is the same failure shape tla-rzvk.4 fixed one level down, arriving
    at the session instead of at the tool.

Also worth one line: 43 of 64 prompts publish a count and 21 do not, and on
the 21 the verdict is now the whole deliverable. Before tla-rzvk.1 those
prompts gave a session nothing and it had to run TLC by hand.

title: Eight phrase assertions over prose files carry a latent false RED
description:
Files: harness/test-deliver-drill.sh

A phrase assertion that greps a prose file line by line goes RED the moment
the phrase it looks for wraps across a line, with nothing wrong in the file
it is checking. The failure direction is a false RED on a correct file, so it
surfaces as a mystery gate break during unrelated work.

MEASURED 2026-10-14 in tla-rzvk.3. Two new rows went red against two files
that both plainly said what the rows asserted. The phrase "leave him the
item's work" had wrapped after the apostrophe. The worker added `flatten`,
`assert_contains_flat`, `assert_matches_flat` and `assert_lacks_flat` and
routed its own 14 phrase rows through them.

THE 8 PRE-EXISTING PHRASE ROWS over drill/study/CLAUDE.md,
drill/study/.claude/commands/check.md and hint.md are still line-based and
carry the same latent break. They pass today because nothing has reflowed
those paragraphs yet. The next edit to any of the three can break the gate
without touching anything the gate is about.

The helpers already exist in the suite. This is routing 8 rows through them
and nothing else. Line-anchored rows stay line-based on purpose, so read
which is which before converting.

THIS IS THE FOURTH INSTANCE OF ONE SHAPE IN ONE SESSION. A line-based scan
over this corpus of prose gives a wrong answer that looks plausible:
  - my 44/64 count of prompts publishing a figure, wrong in five families
  - my 36/28 re-count of the same thing, against the correct 21/43
  - three wrapped claims (can-pyramid 10, altimeter-approx 49, leases 61)
    reading as publishing nothing
  - these two assertion rows
The corpus is prose and prose wraps. Flatten before matching.
close_reason: Nine phrase assertions routed through the flattening helpers at 5adb91d, not the eight the bead predicted. The ninth is a bold lead-in inside a paragraph that reads as a structural label. The partition is complete and stated: 14 already flat, 9 converted, 2 anchored and left, 14 single-token where no wrap can land, summing to the 39 rows over those three files. Each conversion proved four ways, passing on the real file in both forms and reddening only the old form against a deliberately reflowed copy, with the probe extracting the suite's own helper bodies rather than hand-copying them. The suite's output diffs empty before and after at 261 assertions.

title: Should a prompt carrying a possible-table ask the learner to verify it?
description:
Files: drill/control-state/01-slip-on-the-spike/PROMPT.md (and 7 siblings, optional)

FRANK'S CALL, NOT MINE, WHICH IS WHY IT IS FILED RATHER THAN BUILT.

8 prompts state a table of states marked possible and then ask only for a
verdict. control-state/01 is the measured instance: "All of the following
must be possible in your model", four rows, then "run it. Report the verdict."
Nothing asks the learner to check the table against the run, and on that item
the whole lesson hangs on row 3 being legal.

Frank, 2026-10-14: "What I described was an obvious invariant, two people
shouldn't both pick the same thing, and it says as much in the description."
He is right. He did exactly what was asked, got the expected verdict, and had
no reason to test where his rule fired.

tla-rzvk.3 fixes this on the CHECKING side: the session compares a violating
state against the table and says so. That covers all 8 without editing a
prompt and without telegraphing. It only fires when he runs the check.

THE OPEN QUESTION is whether the prompts should ALSO ask for it, which would
make verifying a stated constraint part of the skill being drilled rather than
something the coach catches afterwards. The cost is telegraphing: a line
saying "check your model admits all four rows" points at the table, and on
this item the table IS the trap. I do not think it gives the trap away, since
he still has to find which row his rule misfires on, but that is a judgement
about his learning and not mine to make.

Do not edit any prompt until Frank rules on it.
notes:
FRANK RULED 2026-10-18: "I agree, it does not give it away." So the 8 prompts DO gain the ask. Verifying a stated constraint becomes part of the drilled skill rather than something the coach catches afterwards. The telegraphing cost is accepted: he still has to find which row his rule misfires on. The tla-rzvk.3 checking-side fix stays, the two are complementary. Unblocked.
BUILT AND DELIVERED 2026-10-18 at afe46bd. All eight prompts carry three sentences after the run instruction: "The table above is a claim about your model, not a description of the system. Check every row against it. Say how you checked." Named no row and prescribed no technique. My first scan found six, because two use a different lead-in and only turned up on a scan keyed to the table header. Two of the eight carry rows marked no as well as yes, so "check every row" is deliberate where "check the table admits these" would have been wrong. Seven took the line before their follow-up paragraph, functions-records/06-depot-cover has no follow-up so it took it at the end. Delivered with deliver-drill.sh --refresh-prompts: 8 replaced, 56 left alone, PROGRESS.tsv and LAST-SERVED untouched. A plain delivery would have landed NONE of them, reporting "0 prompt(s) to land, 64 already there", which is the tla-mjvx failure shape exactly.
close_reason: Frank ruled 2026-10-18: 'I agree, it doesn't give it away.' Built and delivered at afe46bd. All eight prompts now ask the learner to check the possible-table, naming no row and prescribing no technique. Delivered via deliver-drill.sh --refresh-prompts, 8 replaced and 56 left alone. Gates: drill style measure 134 assertions, drill corpus static sweep 64 items 0 findings, spelling and pipefail green.

title: Two tlc on PATH, one four releases old, and no gate observes which one a run used
description:
Found by the tla-ytv2.2 author and verified independently by central 2026-10-15.

TWO tlc ARE ON PATH on the author box:

    /home/fkberthold/bin/tlc                      TLC2 Version 2026.07.31.184830 (rev: 30cc360)
    /etc/profiles/per-user/fkberthold/bin/tlc     TLC2 Version 2.19 of 08 August 2024 (rev: 5a47802)

command -v tlc resolves the first, so nothing is wrong today. The second is a nix-profile build four releases behind the pin.

WHY IT MATTERS, AND IT IS NOT JUST PATH ORDER. The pin is observed at INSTALL time and only declared afterwards. scripts/setup:63 carries EXPECT_TLC="2026.07.31" and .github/workflows/verify-puzzles.yml:150 sets the same, so a fresh install verifies the running version and the jar digest. harness/test-toolchain-pin.sh checks the digest on download and that the five declaring sites agree with each other. NOTHING asserts which binary a gate run actually used. So a run against the 2024 build would be silent.

AND THE TWO HAZARDS COMPOSE, which is the part worth acting on. /home/fkberthold/bin/tlc resolves its jar from HOME: line 3 is JAR="$HOME/lib/tla2tools.jar". Every suite here redirects HOME. The tla-ytv2.2 author hit exactly this: its default-roots row pointed HOME at a fixture home, the wrapper could not find its jar, and TLC died with "Could not find or load main class tlc2.TLC" at rc 1 with no count. That read as a parser bug and cost a false red until the fixture symlinked the real jar in. A suite that redirected HOME *and* picked up the nix tlc would not fail at all. It would pass against a 2024 build.

Every empirical constant in V2-PLAN.md section 5 is pinned to 2026.07.31.184830, so a run on another build makes all of them hypotheses again.

THE FIX IS SMALL. Assert the running version once per gate run rather than only at install: read tlc 2>&1, match EXPECT_TLC, and fail loudly naming the binary command -v resolved. scripts/cibuild phase 1 is the natural home since it already claims to be the toolchain-pin phase.

ALSO NOTED, same box, same session: there is no bc. Anything computing a budget ratio has to use awk or shell arithmetic.

Files: scripts/cibuild, harness/test-toolchain-pin.sh

title: Make the study config's read prohibition a gate instead of a contract
description:
drill/study/CLAUDE.md forbids the session from reading under ~/repos/tla-puzzles/drill/, where ANSWER.md, META.md and verify/ live. That is advice, and loom conventions say gate rather than advise. A permissions.deny entry in $DRILL_STUDY_ROOT/.claude/settings.json would make the boundary real.

THE SYNTAX IS NOW KNOWN, which was the tla-ytv2.3 author stated reason for not building it. An absolute path in a permission rule takes a DOUBLE leading slash. Ten real examples on this box, all in allow lists, e.g. Read(//etc/X11/**) and Read(//home/frank/**) in .claude/settings.local.json. So the candidate rule is:

    {"permissions": {"deny": ["Read(//home/fkberthold/repos/tla-puzzles/drill/**)"]}}

VERIFICATION IS THE FIRST STEP AND IT IS NOT OPTIONAL. Every example found is an allow, not a deny, so deny on Read with a recursive glob is unverified here. The author was right that a deny rule which silently matches nothing is worse than honest advice, because it reads as a closed door. Prove it refuses a real Read of drill/state-space/01-clock-never-stops/ANSWER.md from a session started in the study root, and prove the single-slash form fails, before shipping it.

IT IS A PARTIAL GATE EVEN WHEN CORRECT, and the bead should say so rather than overclaim. A deny on the Read tool does not stop Bash cat, and Bash rules match command prefixes rather than paths, so the shell route stays open. What this buys is that the cheap accidental read becomes impossible while the deliberate one stays available. That is still worth having: the failure mode being defended against is a session helpfully opening ANSWER.md while checking an attempt, not Frank deciding to look.

Files: drill/study/.claude/settings.json, harness/test-deliver-drill.sh
notes:
2026-10-14, tla-rzvk: PARTLY DISSOLVED, and do not close it.

Measured on claude 2.1.300: `--tools ""` removes file access entirely. A
one-shot asked to read a file sitting beside it answered CANNOTREAD, and still
loaded CLAUDE.md from the cwd and from a subdirectory of it.

So on the one-shot path (`./drill --check`, `./drill --hint`) the read
prohibition becomes a property of the invocation rather than advice, and both
of this bead's known weaknesses go with it: deny-on-Read was unverified on
this box (all ten local examples are allows) and a Read deny does not stop a
Bash `cat` anyway.

The INTERACTIVE path still has the gap. A session Frank starts by typing
`claude` in a slug directory has full tools and only CLAUDE.md in front of
ANSWER.md, META.md and verify/. That is what this bead still covers, and the
verification-first requirement still stands.

title: No gate checks that an ANSWER.md listing matches the module verify/ runs
description:
Found by the tla-nv5q corpus worker on 2026-10-14 as an incidental divergence in
one item, and widened by central the same day into the gap behind it.

THE MEASURED INSTANCE. drill/sequences/02-floor-robot/ANSWER.md presents a
listing that names Tiles and NoTileTwice. Every module and config in that item's
verify/ names Cells and NoCellTwice:

  ANSWER.md:9    Tiles == (1..3) \X (1..3)
  ANSWER.md:42   NoTileTwice == \A i, j \in DOMAIN path : ...
  ANSWER.md:51   NoTileTwice, listed as the config's invariant

  RobotRef.tla:7    Cells == (1..3) \X (1..3)
  RobotRef.tla:42   NoCellTwice == \A i, j \in DOMAIN path : ...
  RobotRef.cfg:5    NoCellTwice

Confirmed present on main at b748d21, so it predates today's work and is not a
spelling artifact. The listing is still a correct spec, so a reader who copies it
gets something that checks. It is just not the thing the gate verified, and the
invariant name a reader is told to put in a cfg is not the one the real cfg uses.

THE GAP BEHIND IT. All 64 drill ANSWER.md files carry a fenced code block, and
nothing compares any of them to the module the gate runs.

  grep -c '^```' over drill/*/[0-9]*/ANSWER.md  -> all 64 carry one
  answer_code() at harness/drill-gate.sh:1027-1040 is the only reader of those
  blocks, and its single caller at :1545 uses it for ONE purpose: the telegraph
  floor, which checks whether a token in the answer's code also appears in
  PROMPT.md. It never looks at verify/.

So the listing is the artifact a reader actually copies, and it is the one part
of an item that no check reads for correctness. Same family as tla-ywf4, which
found the distinct-state counts unguarded: ANSWER.md carries claims and the gate
only ever checked the exit codes.

A BYTE COMPARE IS THE WRONG CHECK and would fail on every item. A listing
legitimately differs from its module: the module carries a header comment and a
MODULE line, the listing often omits the config, and several items show a

title: 24 lines of harness cross-reference by line number, none gated
description:
Raised by the tla-o14p worker on 2026-10-14 after the constraint changed how it
made its edit, and measured by central the same day.

THE SHAPE. Harness files cite each other by line number in comments, and nothing
checks any of them. A net line change in a cited file silently invalidates every
reference below the edit, and the first symptom is a reader following a pointer
to the wrong code.

MEASURED. 24 citing lines carrying 17 distinct targets:

  grep -rn 'drill-gate\.sh:[0-9]\|completion-gate\.sh:[0-9]\|reading-gate\.sh:[0-9]\|verdict\.sh:[0-9]' harness/ scripts/ | wc -l
  -> 24

  by target file: drill-gate.sh 14, verdict.sh 9, reading-gate.sh 2

NONE IS CURRENTLY OUT OF RANGE. Every distinct target line number is within its
file's length, checked by script. That is a weak result and worth saying plainly:
a reference can point at the wrong line inside the file and this check cannot see
it. The strong claim available today is only that nothing points past the end.

Two of the fourteen point INSIDE the comment block tla-o14p rewrote:
  completion-gate.sh:180  "harness/drill-gate.sh:1064-1073's line format unchanged"
  completion-gate.sh:421  "Same pattern as harness/drill-gate.sh:1071-1073"
Nine more point below it: completion-gate.sh:284, :307, :437, :481,
test-completion-gate.sh:566, reading-gate.sh:113, :212, :342, :552,
test-indeterminate.sh:215, :222, :634.

Central verified both of the first two still land after the o14p rewrite:
drill-gate.sh:1064 reads "# waivers <meta.md>: lines of the form" and :1071-1073
is the waivers() body. They held because the worker made its rewrite
line-count-neutral ON PURPOSE, six lines out and six in, which cost it a sentence
it wanted to keep. That is the cost this bead is about: the convention now
constrains how every future edit to drill-gate.sh may be written.

WHY THIS IS THE GATE-DON'T-ADVISE SHAPE. loom-conventions.md: every
drift-detector or correctness check must be wired to a real enforcement gate,
never left as an advisory a human has to remember. A line-numbered pointer is an
assertion about another file, and here there are 24 of them with no gate.

THREE WAYS OUT, and the third is the one central would take.

O1. Gate the numbers. A static suite that parses every <file>:<line> reference
and checks the target line still matches a recorded fingerprint. Precise, and it
makes every intentional line change a two-file edit.

O2. Drop the numbers and cite by name. "see waivers() in harness/drill-gate.sh"
needs no gate because a function rename breaks the grep anyway. Loses the
precision for references that point at a specific comment rather than a function.

O3. Cite by name where a name exists, gate the rest. Most of the 24 point at a
named function or a keyword, so they convert for free. The residue that genuinely
points at prose gets a fingerprint assertion. Smallest gate, least constraint on
future edits.

ONE THING TO DO FIRST EITHER WAY. tla-ywf4's gate half adds lines to
drill-gate.sh, so some of the fourteen will go stale as it lands. Its brief asks
it to report every reference it invalidated with the corrected number. Fix those
from its report before building anything here, otherwise this bead starts from a
corpus that is already wrong.

description:
AUTOFAN-EXCLUDE: prose judgment across 64 items, one reader, not a parallel wave.

Depends on the ruling recorded on tla-0yis, 2026-10-14. That bead ruled the
general question and fixed the two clear failures. This is the sweep.

THE TEST, as ruled: does removing the sentence leave the item underdetermined?
Keep it if the prompt cannot pose its problem or publish a reproducible count
without it. Cut it if the reader could have reached the answer from the rest and
the sentence only shortens the search.

WHY A SWEEP IS NEEDED RATHER THAN TRUST. Three workers on 2026-10-14 ranked
their own three families and found the shape in roughly half the items they
looked at. Five families have never been ranked at all: core, control-state,
state-space, sets, temporal. The gate cannot see any of this, since every one of
these prompts passes check 1 clean with no operator token on the page.

ALREADY JUDGED BY CENTRAL, do not re-derive, recorded in full on tla-0yis:
  PASSES   functions-records/06-depot-cover, modules/06, modules/03 (marginal)
  FAILS    modules/08 (mildly), sequences/03-returns-desk (forecloses nothing)
  FIXED    sequences/07-pneumatic-tube, modules/07-the-hoist-and-the-crates
  UNSEEN   sequences/04, sequences/08, functions-records/05

NEVER RANKED: all of core, control-state, state-space, sets and temporal. 40
items.

THE REMEDY WHEN AN ITEM FAILS is not simply to delete the sentence. The authors
kept these on purpose, so that a reader who gets stuck has something to check.
The substitution the sequences/07 fix used is the pattern: cut the hint, state
the model, publish the count, and let the count do the foreclosing. That works
only where a wrong-but-clean neighbour exists in verify/ with a different count.
Where no such neighbour exists, say so rather than removing the reader's only
foothold.

foreclosing row is a published count should not be relying on an unchecked
number.

title: No gate checks a distinct-state count, so every one is an unguarded claim
description:
Found by the sets worker on 2026-10-14 and independently relied on by the
modules worker, which measured every count by hand because the gate does not.

THE GAP. harness/drill-gate.sh check 2 compares exit codes only. It runs every
verify module through harness/verdict.sh and asserts the rc matches the one
ANSWER.md records (drill-gate.sh:1831-1836). It never reads a distinct-state
count, a generated-state count or a depth, so every one of those numbers in
every META.md, ANSWER.md and PROMPT.md across 64 items is an unguarded claim.

WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN AN rc. The count is the FORECLOSING ROW. A drill
prompt publishes the expected distinct-state count so a reader can tell their
answer is wrong without being told why, and several items lean on the count as
the whole diagnosis. drill/core/01-box-office/ANSWER.md says it outright: under
a channel with deadlock checking off, "the state count is the whole diagnosis".
So a stale count is worse than a stale rc, because it is what the learner
checks against.

AND THE COUNTS DRIFT FOR A DIFFERENT REASON THAN THE rcs DO. An rc is coarse
and survives a small spec change. A count moves on any change to the constants,
the state space or the initial predicate, and it moves silently.

MEASURED STATE TODAY, so the bead starts from a known-good baseline rather than
a suspicion. Two workers checked their families by hand on 2026-10-14 and every
figure reproduced:

  modules    all figures in both the ANSWER tables and the PROMPT tables, plus
             item 02's claim that the trace is seven states long
  sets       all 46, including the five counts the prompts quote (50, 61, 274,
             321, 398)

So the corpus is correct today and nothing guards it tomorrow. That is the
gate-don't-advise shape: a correctness invariant resting on somebody
remembering to check it.

ONE DECLARED EXCEPTION TO CARRY INTO THE FIX. drill/sets/03-ballast's
BallastAnyStart records 1 distinct state and TLC prints no count at all,
because the invariant is violated during initial-state computation.
drill/sets/03-ballast/ANSWER.md:90 declares the 1 as the one state in the
trace. Any checker has to treat a missing count on an initial-state violation
as that declared convention rather than a mismatch.

THE EXTRACTION IS ALREADY WRITTEN, twice, so this is not new work from nothing:
  sed -n 's/.* \([0-9][0-9]*\) distinct states found.*/\1/p' <log> | tail -n 1
is the form in drill/control-state/verify-all.sh, and
drill/temporal/verify-item.sh prints the count as its fourth column. Both read
the LAST match on purpose, because a liveness run prints the same number on a
progress line too.

Note this interacts with tla-tkdh, which consolidates those helper scripts. The
count reader should land in the surviving driver rather than in a fifth place.

          grep -l '^## Gate rows' drill/*/[0-9]*/ANSWER.md -> the 16, exactly
          modules/01-08 and state-space/01-08
          grep -c distinct ... -> the 6 temporal items with none, plus

SO THE FIX IS a distinct column on 16 Gate rows tables, plus the gate check.

AND STATE-SPACE'S PROSE TABLES STAY. Tables like "| without symmetry | 0 | 37 |"
and "| run | rc | distinct | depth | wall |" are narrative about what the item
teaches, not the gate's contract. Reconciling them against measurements would
have been a large wrong edit. The two families differ because modules and
state-space run one spec under many configs and need a wrapper module per gate
row, while the other six already have one module per run.

THE PARSER SHAPE: anchored on the keyword, tolerant on the value, which is what
rc_claims at drill-gate.sh:1137-1200 already does for exit codes. Header cells
vary across the corpus ("distinct", "distinct states") and value cells vary too
("4", "63", "129 found"). So find the header cell containing "distinct", take
that column index, read the first integer from the cell. Some tables also carry
"generated" and "depth" columns, same mechanism and worth doing in the same pass.

A row whose rc is 150 or 255 never reaches state enumeration, so its cell is a
literal "-", not a number and not empty.

NOT BLOCKED ON tla-tkdh, contrary to this bead's last paragraph. The gate drives
TLC through its own parallel job runner and writes its own .rc files, so a .count
file beside them is gate-internal. tkdh consolidates the family DEV helpers,
which is a different program. The two can land in either order.

   declaration or it will report an unreadable log as a failure.

3. THE DECLARED-1 CONVENTION FROM drill/sets/03-ballast DID NOT APPLY TO ANY OF
   THE 16 DASH ROWS. All 16 were audited for the shape and every one came back
   with no trace-state line, so none is an initial-state violation with a
   suppressed count. The convention still has to be handled for sets/03 itself.

4. DO NOT ENUMERATE WRAPPERS WITH A G-PREFIX GLOB.
   drill/modules/05-the-helper-that-leaked/verify/ holds Gearing.tla and
   GearingLocal.tla as ordinary helper modules, so the glob yields 6 wrappers
   against 4 gate rows. The two authorities that agree are the ANSWER.md table
   and the same-stem cfg. Checked both directions: all 79 rows have a same-stem
   .tla and .cfg, and no G<digit><digit>*.cfg in the 32 verify/ directories
   lacks a gate row.

AND ONE PARSER HAZARD THE NEW COLUMN CREATES. rc_claims at
drill-gate.sh:1133-1180 falls back to a bare pipe-delimited digit cell when its
rc and exit arms both miss, and it takes the LAST such match on the line. The
new distinct cell is bare digits sitting after the rc cell, so a count parser
written the same way would inherit that fallback, and a row that ever lost its
"rc N" text would read its distinct count as an rc. Key the count parse on the
distinct header cell or on column position after rc, not on a bare-digit scan.
Every row carries "rc N" today, so nothing is broken: the 78-job queue parsed
every rc correctly after the change.

All 16 tables now carry the identical header "| module | rc | distinct | stands
for |". The format is uniform across both families.

GATE HALF LANDED 2026-10-14, merged, plus 8e804b2 for the two waivers.

253 count claims parse, 251 compare against a measured count, 2 waived.
EVERY ONE OF THE 251 MATCHED. The corpus's numbers were already right and only
unguarded, which is the same result the corpus half got on its 24 prose figures.
Full gate at -P 4: 64 items, 0 findings, 0 unchecked, 1 declared, VERDICT OK,
66 to 68 s over 422 TLC jobs.

harness/test-drill.sh 161 -> 184 assertions, --static 4 -> 5. Six RED assertions
watched fail first. scripts/test unaffected by budget: the fast drill row read
3.3 s against a 3.0 s budget and still passed, since the nudge needs 3x plus 5 s.
No BUDGET DRIFT block.

TWO COUNT WAIVERS WERE NEEDED, NOT ONE. Central predicted sets/03-ballast and
missed the second:

  drill/core/04-lift-types  NegativeInConfig  rc 255, ConfigFileException before
  the state graph, no count in the log, ANSWER.md:109 records 0.

Central's own 79-gate-row measurement missed it because that item's table is six
columns wide rather than the four-column ## Gate rows shape, so it was never in
the sample. Re-measured independently by central: rc 255, zero "distinct states"
lines, ConfigFileException. Both waivers now live in META.md and are echoed.

THE CORPUS HAS 20 DISTINCT TABLE HEADERS CARRYING THE WORD, NOT THREE SHAPES, and
two of them break a naive parser:

  drill/state-space/01-clock-never-stops:43  carries the word TWICE in one
  header, as "spec-side distinct" and "constraint distinct". Reading the last
  matching cell takes the wrong column.
  drill/core/03-bakery-obligations:129  is a DATA row ending "rc 0, 78
  generated, 40 distinct". Treating any pipe row containing the word as a header
  invents a column for a table that has none.

The discriminator that handles both, and it was not in central's brief: a header
is a pipe row whose NEXT line is the separator. Anchor on that.

SO CENTRAL'S "40 ITEMS" COUNT IS 39 PLUS ONE EXCEPTION.
drill/core/03-bakery-obligations has no distinct column at all. Its six modules
record no count and correctly raise no finding.

AN ESCAPED PIPE INSIDE A TABLE CELL.
drill/control-state/08-wrong-label:72 carries a literal \| in a cell, and a naive
pipe split shifts every later column by one. That table has no distinct column
today, which is luck rather than a guarantee. The parser parks the escape under
\001 and restores it.

THE BARE-DIGIT HAZARD IS NARROWER THAN CENTRAL FEARED, measured rather than
assumed. rc_claims' lastmatch advances past RLENGTH, so matches are
non-overlapping and the separator pipe is consumed: "| 0 | 7 |" yields only
"| 0 |". A two-cell rc-then-distinct row reads its rc correctly even with no
"rc N" text. It would still bite on an odd cell count, so the column anchor
stayed and no second instance was added.

"LAST MATCH WINS" NEEDED CHECKING. A sweep over all 64 items found 3 stems hit in
two tables each, all in drill/modules/01-two-tanks-one-hose, config-keyed at :192
and gate-rows at :207. All 3 agreed, so no precedence rule is load-bearing on
today's corpus. That is a fact about today rather than a guarantee.

A WARM --changed-only CACHE LEGITIMATELY COMPARES ZERO COUNTS. The claim is in
the cache key and a key is recorded only when both halves matched, so zero
comparisons is the right answer there. The first draft warned on it. The warning
now excludes cached_n > 0 and the block says why.

PIPEFAIL MEASURED, NOT REASONED. Over a 14 MB log with 200,001 matches,
grep -oE ... | tail -1 | cut returned rc 0 on six consecutive runs. The probe was
sensitive: | head -1 over the same log returned 141. No match returned 1 and an
absent file returned 2, both yielding the empty string the parent reads as no
measurement. harness/test-pipefail.sh passes 25 assertions and | tail is not on
its ban list.

Parser anchors on a header row whose next line is the separator, which is what handles state-space/01's doubled column word and core/03's data row containing it. Runner keeps its log and writes a count beside its rc, and the job cache key carries the claim. Two count-waivers in META.md, commit 8e804b2. Full gate 64 items 0 findings at -P4 in 66s. title: Two sibling gates read telegraph-waiver from different files
description:
Found by the sets worker on 2026-10-14, which read the gate rather than
trusting central's brief. The brief said META.md and was wrong for drill.

THE SPLIT, both verified:

  harness/drill-gate.sh:1432       wv="$(waivers "$answer")"      -> ANSWER.md
  harness/completion-gate.sh:699   wv="$(waiver_lines "$meta")"   -> META.md

Same keyword, same syntax, same reason-length floor, read from two different
files by two gates written days apart. An author who works both channels files
a waiver the gate never sees, and nothing reports it: a waiver that is not
found is silence, not a finding.

THE DRILL SIDE IS THE ODD ONE on the argument. completion-gate.sh:511 raises
SHAPE-NO-META with the reason "no META.md; it is where a telegraph-waiver lives
and where the constructs are declared", so the completion gate states its
choice in a finding message. The drill gate's own documentation at
drill-gate.sh:1065-1073 describes the syntax without naming the file, which is
how the brief got it wrong.

THE ARGUMENT FOR META.md. A waiver is a claim about the ITEM's design, next to
the constructs it declares, and META.md is the file the gate already treats as
the item's own statement about itself. ANSWER.md is the reference solution, and
a waiver is not part of an answer.

THE ARGUMENT FOR ANSWER.md. The drill gate's telegraph check compares the
prompt against the answer, so the answer is what the check is reading anyway.

Recommendation is META.md for both, since one of the two gates already says so
in a user-facing message and the completion channel's nine items already carry
their waivers there. That makes the drill gate the one that moves.

WHAT MOVING IT COSTS. Nothing today: no drill item in the 64 on main carries a
telegraph-waiver line at all. Four workers on 2026-10-14 each declined to add
one, with the modules worker giving the reason: a waiver suppresses a flagged
token, nothing was flagged, so a waiver would plant a permanent WAIVER line
against no finding. So the fix is one line plus a test, and it has no corpus
migration behind it. Do it before any item needs a waiver rather than after.

harness/test-drill.sh and harness/test-completion-gate.sh both gate waiver
handling, so whichever side moves needs its fixture moved with it.

Files: harness/drill-gate.sh, harness/test-drill.sh
notes:
RULED 2026-10-14 by Frank: META.md for both, so the drill gate moves. Central's
recommendation taken unchanged.

Verified before dispatch: meta="${item}/META.md" is already assigned at
drill-gate.sh:1401, so the change at :1431 is one token and nothing new comes
into scope.

Verified: no drill item on main carries a telegraph-waiver line, so there is no
corpus migration.

TWO THINGS ADDED TO THE SCOPE beyond the one-token change.

First, the comment block at drill-gate.sh:1065-1073 is the root cause and gets
rewritten to name the file. It documents the waiver syntax without saying which
file it reads from, which is why central briefed four workers with the wrong file
on 2026-10-14 and why the split survived days. Fixing the call without fixing the
comment leaves the next author in the same position.

Second, a NEGATIVE test. The existing fixture only proves the gate reads whichever
file it is pointed at, so moving the source back would pass the suite again. The
new assertion is that a waiver planted in ANSWER.md is NOT honoured, so the token
it names still raises its telegraph finding.

Design drawer: drawer_tla_puzzles_decisions_1129be84450b30408259bfb1

LANDED 2026-10-14. Gate change in the merge of 0619c98, the corpus migration in
d4d49ae.

CENTRAL'S COST CLAIM WAS WRONG AND THE WORKER CAUGHT IT. Two drill items DID
carry a telegraph-waiver, both in ANSWER.md, so the fix had a corpus migration
after all:

  drill/state-space/02-four-identical-workers/ANSWER.md:126
  drill/state-space/06-liveness-at-the-fence/ANSWER.md:119

Both landed 2026-10-12 in d524ce6 with the state-space family. The claim that no
item carried one came from the four authors of the 2026-10-14 wave each declining
to add one, generalised to the whole corpus without searching it. That wave never
covered the family that shipped two days earlier. It is the one-surface failure
CLAUDE.md names: a real surface searched, and the search stopped there.

Worse, it was already in hand. The tla-ywf4 corpus-half worker's report listed
both waivers as "two pre-existing WAIVER lines for the TLC telegraph token in
state-space/02 and state-space/06". Central read that line and did not connect it
to the cost claim in the sibling brief.

The worker proved the migration on a copy rather than writing into a sibling's
territory, and stopped. Right call. Central moved both lines into META.md under a
## Telegraph waiver heading and re-gated: 64 items, 0 findings, 0 unchecked, both
waivers echoed from the new home.

PLACEMENT IS SAFE, and the reason is worth keeping. meta_constructs at
drill-gate.sh:1101-1131 sets insec only on a heading whose squeezed letters
contain "construct", and prints only bullet lines while insec is set. A
## Telegraph waiver heading clears it and the bare keyword line is not a bullet,
so nothing leaks into check 3's construct count.

TEST COUNTS: harness/test-drill.sh went from 159 to 161 assertions, part 1f from
5 to 7. The new negative assertion is that a waiver planted in ANSWER.md is not
honoured, which bites when the call is reverted. Confirmed red before green.

ONE THING FOR WHOEVER EDITS drill-gate.sh NEXT, filed separately as its own bead:
four harness files carry 14 line-numbered cross-references into drill-gate.sh and
nothing gates any of them. Two point inside the comment block this bead rewrote.
The worker made the rewrite line-count-neutral to avoid invalidating them, which
cost it a sentence it wanted to keep.

One token at drill-gate.sh:1431, plus the comment block that caused this by never naming the file, plus a negative assertion that a waiver planted in ANSWER.md is not honoured. The cost claim in the brief was wrong: two state-space items carried waivers from 2026-10-12, migrated in commit d4d49ae. Gate reads 64 items, 0 findings, all waivers echoed.
